text:
DHA Director Navy Vice Adm. Darin Via is positioning medical planning, data and continuous learning as core components of future combat support

The agency proposed a Joint Warfighter Health System covering mental health, TBI and infectious disease

Learn more about the agency’s modernization priorities at the 2026 Healthcare Summit on Dec. 3

Defense Health Agency Director Navy Vice Adm. Darin Via is emphasizing data-driven planning and continuous learning as the military medical enterprise prepares for increasingly complex combat environments, the agency reported Tuesday.

As the Defense Health Agency advances data-driven medical planning, AI and new approaches to warfighter health, the 2026 Healthcare Summit on Dec. 3 will explore how modernization can strengthen readiness—and highlight contract opportunities supporting the future of military healthcare. Sign up now to secure your seat.

How Is DHA Using the Joint Medical Planning Tool for Future Combat Planning?

Speaking at a recent conference for military healthcare professionals, Via emphasized the need to identify ways to return injured service members to duty more quickly while improving access to care, referrals and measurable readiness outcomes.

He highlighted the Joint Medical Planning Tool, or JMPT, a computer-based simulation as an important capability for supporting casualty forecasting, treatment and evacuation decisions, and supply planning for future conflicts.

“To achieve our North Star, DHA should be synchronized and data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support,” Via said.

In an August request for information, DHA sought industry input on modernizing its Joint Operational Medical Information System, or JOMIS, medical planning and modeling capabilities. The effort would address limitations in existing tools, including the Joint Medical Planning Tool and Medical Planners Toolkit, and provide more dynamic ways to model medical demand and operational resources.

What Role Does the Joint Trauma System Play in DHA’s Approach?

DHA is also working to improve its support for combatant commands and casualty receiving facilities by establishing medical supply requirements, using planning tools to estimate casualty volumes and preparing additional space inside military hospitals and clinics.

Via identified the Joint Trauma System as a model for how DHA can use operational experience and data to foster continuous improvement in military medicine.

The tool provides a framework for establishing common trauma care practices and using clinical data and lessons learned to improve care across the joint force.

“Military medicine faces a more complex future than it did during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan,” Via said. “The enemy has changed the tactics on us, and we have to adapt.”.

What Is the Planned Joint Warfighter Health System?

DHA intends to apply lessons from the Joint Trauma System beyond battlefield trauma by establishing a Joint Warfighter Health System.

Via said the new system will use the same continuous, data-driven process improvement approach to address a broader range of conditions affecting military readiness.

“We’re going to use those same models to drive mental health, TBI (traumatic brain injury), and infectious disease,” he added.

text:
By MOAA Staff

The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act can do “a ton of good” for millions in the veteran community, MOAA’s top official told a CNN audience Sept. 9 … but only if lawmakers vote on the bill before the end of the 119th Congress.

Lt. Gen. Brian T. Kelly, USAF (Ret), appeared on CNN News Central to review the contents of the omnibus legislation and encourage lawmakers to move the landmark legislation forward.

“The worst thing that could happen is no vote before this Congress goes out,” Kelly told anchor Brianna Keilar during the live studio interview in Washington, D.C. “If that happens, everybody’s back to square one. They’ve got to reintroduce all this legislation, and all the waiting continues. …

“We’re all looking to and counting on Congress to take the politics out of this, take emotion out of this, and if you put the veteran at the center ... you have a vote.”

[SHARING THEIR STORIES: These Veterans, Caregivers, and Survivors Are Among the Millions Supported by TCAVA]

The legislation contains more than 60 individual bills, many of which address critical MOAA priorities such as:

Relief for nearly 60,000 combat-injured military retirees who face an unjust pay offset between their military retirement pay and VA disability compensation. “The fact that those are offset to each other while others are allowed to keep both of those things is really unjust, particularly if you think about who’s most deserving,” Kelly said. “Why wouldn’t we as a country say those at the front of the line ought to be our combat-injured?”

Short- and long-term support for military caregivers, including provisions that would provide financial, professional, and mental health resources.

Removal of restrictions faced by military survivors who lose benefits if they remarry before age 55. Kelly called the existing rules “archaic,” adding, “Those benefits were earned for those folks, and they should be able to keep them.”

The bill also improves survivor benefits, boosts VA research and suicide-prevention efforts, expands VA transition and education resources, and much more.

Kelly said the bill would do “a ton of good for tens of millions of veterans, their families, caregivers, survivors, in one opportunity” and said that good outweighed the legislation’s funding mechanism, which comes from changes to VA disability rating schedule for sleep apnea and tinnitus that are already in the works.

“You never get a perfect bill,” Kelly told Keilar. “In totality … this is worth it.”

MOAA in The Hill

The interview came less than a week after a commentary piece on the bill authored by Kelly appeared on The Hill’s website with a similar message.

“Backing this bill, imperfections and all, is not a political act; it is a pragmatic one,” Kelly wrote for the D.C.-based news outlet. “It honors the current service members and veterans who gave so much, the caregivers and families who carry the weight beside them, and the survivors who keep their memory alive.”

text:
By Bernard S. Little Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, Hospital Communications

Suicide prevention help and education are readily available at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center 24/7 for service members, families, other beneficiaries of the Military Health System (MHS) and staff members.

Walter Reed joins military communities around the globe in observing Suicide Prevention Month during September as part of the Department of War's 2026 campaign, “Joining Your Fight: Connect to Protect.” The campaign reinforces suicide prevention and response, which are vital components of optimizing the performance of the Total Force and readiness.

“Walter Reed provides multiple pathways for suicide prevention and support, including emergency and crisis response, mental healthcare, counseling, peer support, resilience services, chaplain support, training, and command outreach,” said U.S. Army Maj. Ajus Ninan, of Addiction Treatment Services, Directorate of Mental Health at Walter Reed.

U.S. Army Chaplain (Maj.) Young H. Kim, chaplain clinician and resource manager in the Department of Pastoral Care (DPC) at Walter Reed, agreed. He added that DPC staff works with other agencies across the medical center and DOW in support of suicide prevention, including Military and Family Support Center (also referred to as Military and Family Readiness Center, or Fleet and Family Support Center -- FFSC), National Intrepid Center of Excellence, inpatient and outpatient mental healthcare services, Military OneSource, Psychological Heath Resource Center, the inTransition Program, and others.

“There are also numerous resources available within the National Capital Region,” Kim said. “There is an on-call duty chaplain available 24/7 to respond to any staff or beneficiaries for any crisis that are contributing factors to suicide.”

The DPC also offers the quarterly workshops Applied Suicide Intervention Skills Training (ASIST) and safeTALK (Suicide Alertness for Everyone: Tell, Ask, Listen, [and] KeepSafe). “These workshops can also be provided at any time upon request,” Kim shared. He described the ASIST workshop as “an immersive, two-day interactive course designed to teach suicide first-aid.”

He said safeTALK is a half-day suicide alertness training facilitated by DPC to teach participants how to recognize signs of suicide and connect individuals to life-saving resources.

“There is also service-specific suicide prevention training available anytime upon request by tenant units,” Kim said. “DPC staff chaplains also offer spiritual resiliency training on various topics in partnership with the Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) every Friday at 10 a.m.”

Preventing suicides

“One of the most effective ways to prevent suicide is to instill resiliency skills into our staff members and beneficiaries at Walter Reed to help cope with life’s challenges before they become contributing factors to suicide,” said Kim. “The Army and Navy offer workshops and retreats for service members and their families to promote effective life skills and enhance healthier relationships through CREDO -- Chaplains Religious Enrichment Development Operation, and BSRT -- Building Strong and Ready Teams, programs which are offered quarterly.”

Ninan added that suicide prevention services offered at Walter Reed also include the FFSC’s Suicide Awareness and Prevention/ACT Training. ACT stands for Ask (directly about suicide), Care (by listening without judgment and demonstrate concern), and Treat (by immediately connecting the individual to appropriate help).

“This training helps participants identify warning signs, respond to individuals who may be at risk, and locate available support resources,” Ninan explained.

“The FFSC also provides life skills education that help strengthen protective factors and address stressors before they develop into a crisis,” Ninan said. Topics covered during the classes include stress and anger management, communication and relationship skills, parenting, conflict resolution, team building, grief and loss, work-life balance, goal setting and time management.

FFSC classes are routinely scheduled and can also be offered at command locations on request, Ninan added. Commands and individuals should contact the FFSC at 301-319-4087 for dates, registration, and unit-specific training requests.

Ninan added that REACH (Resources Exist, Asking Can Help), a Defense Suicide Prevention Office facilitator-led suicide-prevention training is available online at https://www.dspo.mil/Home/Tools/REACH/.

Also, the Uniformed Services University’s (USU) Consortium for Defense Psychology (CDP) offers recurring online suicide-prevention education for mental healthcare providers, prescribing providers, and mental health technicians (MHTs), said Ninan. For more information about the CDP, visit https://cdp.usuhs.edu/training-schedule.

‘Suicide is complex’

“Suicide is complex and generally does not result from one event, one diagnosis, one job, one deployment, or military service alone,” Ninan stated.

Someone unexpectedly saying goodbye, giving away possessions, suddenly putting affairs in order or making final arrangements, warrants attention, Kim explained. If someone begins seeking access to firearms, medications or other potentially lethal means, experiencing sudden anger or violent outbursts, displaying little concern for the safety of oneself or others, these are likely indicators that a person may be in crisis and are experiencing suicidal thoughts. “Some clear indicators also include if someone is talking or writing about a wish to die, suicide, or hurting themselves.”

“Some indicators that may not be obvious include expressing feelings of hopelessness, feeling trapped, displays or expressions of guilt and/or shame, feeling like a burden, withdrawal and isolation from others, reckless and impulsive behavior, increased substance abuse, and significant stressors, including relationship, financial, health and/or work challenges, and any loss-related difficulties (death, job, etc.),” Kim added.

“What we teach at the ASIST workshop is that these are ‘invitations’ for others to be caring enough to explore,” Kim said. “Anything can be an invitation of a person with thoughts of suicide for others to approach and explore what that invitation is all about. It’s better that someone explore an invitation and confirm it’s not suicide than not explore and face the consequences of losing someone to suicide.”

Ninan agreed, adding, “Most, but not all, people who die by suicide exhibit warning signs. Do not wait for certainty. If something does not seem right, check in and ask directly.”

He urged people to ask those for whom they have a concern, “Are you thinking about killing yourself?” “Are you thinking about ending your life?” “Do you have a plan to hurt yourself?”

“Asking directly about suicide does not put the idea in someone’s head. A supportive conversation can help the person express what they are experiencing and get help,” Ninan said.

“Care, remain calm, listen without judgment, express concern, and tell the person that help is available,” Ninan said. “Do not leave the person alone. Call 911 if there is immediate danger, if a weapon is present, if a suicide attempt is occurring, or if the situation is potentially life-threatening. Call 988, then press 1, or text 838255 for the Veterans/Military Crisis Line. Escort or connect the person to emergency care, a medical professional, mental healthcare provider, chaplain, trusted leader, or qualified crisis support, and continue to check in after the immediate crisis.”

“Be a listening ear with non-judgmental attitude to assure the person that they are not alone and that you care and help is available,” Kim agreed.

Don’t wait; suicide is preventable

“Don’t wait until you encounter someone thinking about suicide to gather various resources,” said Kim. “We can get closer to building safer communities if more people learn to identify and assist those who may be at risk of suicide before they act. Lifeguards can only be effective if they are right by the person drowning. Suicide caregivers are most effective if they are close by and available for the person with thoughts of suicide to reach out in time of need. CPR is taught for the very purpose of being prepared and able to apply immediate first-aid measures to resuscitate someone who stops breathing until the paramedics arrive to help. Suicide first-aid like ASIST (Applied Suicide Intervention Skills Training), can be taught and are very effective in preventing suicide.”

“Suicide is preventable,” added Ninan. “It’s a shared responsibility among leaders, supervisors, peers, families, chaplains, medical professionals, mental healthcare providers, counselors, and community members. All have a role in reducing the stigma and helping people seek support early. No one should face a crisis alone.”

text:
Genito-urological Injuries Increased in Warfighters After 2001

WASHINGTON — Nearly 2,000 U.S. troops suffered debilitating injuries to their groins or genitals during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan between 2000 and 2013, and about 307,000 more sustained some type of head injury over the same period, all injuries that can compromise fertility and sexual function. Those figures illustrate the stakes behind family-planning decisions made ahead of a combat deployment and motivate a new Pentagon program that will help troops preserve before they deploy their ability to have children.

A notice published in the Federal Register on Aug. 13 announced that the DoD will launch a 3-year demonstration project on Sept. 14 that reimburses eligible active-duty servicemembers for the cost of freezing sperm or eggs. The benefit will cover up to $500 a year in sperm cryopreservation costs. The reimbursement rises to $10,000 a year for egg, or oocyte, cryopreservation, reflecting the far higher cost and complexity of egg retrieval, which typically requires hormone stimulation and a surgical procedure, compared with sperm banking.

The program, required by Section 709 of the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025, is open to active-duty members of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force and Space Force who meet at least one of three conditions. These include receiving orders for an assignment that qualifies for hazardous duty pay, being likely to receive such orders within 120 days or being separated from a spouse, domestic partner or dating partner for 180 days or more under orders, including sea duty.

Participation is voluntary. Eligible troops can obtain preservation services either at a military treatment facility with a reproductive medicine program or through a civilian clinic of their choosing. Reimbursable costs include gamete retrieval procedures and the medications and lab testing associated with them, cryopreservation itself and the shipping and storage of the samples for the duration of the 3-year demonstration.

Because the Defense Health Agency does not have visibility into deployment orders, commanders must validate a servicemember’s eligibility before reimbursement is approved. Troops must submit a complete DHA Form 459, along with itemized invoices, within 120 days of the date services began, typically the date of retrieval or the associated lab procedure or prescription. Servicemembers could be eligible for reimbursement more than once during the 3-year pilot, if they again meet the eligibility criteria.

Participants also will be required to attest that they have an advance medical directive specifying what should happen to their preserved gametes in the event of their death. Decisions about continued storage, disposition or future use after the demonstration period remain solely the responsibility of the servicemember and fall outside the scope of the program, according to the notice.

The program has been more than a decade in coming. In 2016, then-Defense Secretary Ash Carter announced a similar pilot as part of a broader package of family-friendly policies, saying the department wanted to help troops preserve their ability to start a family even after a combat injury. That earlier program never got off the ground. This time, the effort comes with a congressional mandate and a defined evaluation plan: The Pentagon will track how many servicemembers use the benefit, its total cost, the administrative burden of running it and its effects on force readiness, retention and member satisfaction during the pilot period.

Military families and support organizations have pushed for such benefits for years. Improvised explosive devices (IEDs) were the signature weapon of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, causing thousands of severe combat casualties and complex, multi-system trauma. Among the most devastating were urotrauma and pelvic injuries. Severe blast winds and ground-strike detonations caused devastating damage to the pelvis, urinary tract, and reproductive organs.

In a 2023 study, a Rutgers University research team used predefined search criteria to primarily identify any casualties that arrived at a military treatment facility with urological-based injuries. The found that the registry contained 25,897 adult casualties, of which 7.2% sustained urological injuries.1

The median age for injury was 25, and explosive injuries (64%) and firearms (27%) were the primary causes. Most patients survived until hospital discharge (94%). The authors pointed out that the most frequently injured organs were the scrotum (60%), testes (53%), penis (30%), and kidneys (30%).

“The incidence of genitourinary trauma persistently increased for both military and civilian personnel as the U.S. remained actively engaged in major military conflicts during this period,” the study concluded. “Patients with genitourinary trauma in this data set were often associated with high injury severity scores and required an increased number of immediate and long-term resources for survival and rehabilitation.”

The injuries weren’t just immediate and physical, however. In 2014, the Bob Woodruff Foundation convened a conference examining how combat injuries affect intimacy and family planning, and many nonprofits have offered free or discounted cryopreservation services to some servicemembers in the interim. Until now, however, deploying servicemembers who wanted to bank sperm or eggs as a hedge against combat injury or prolonged separation have had to pay for it themselves, and some military families have described going to considerable lengths, including seeking emergency cryopreservation after a servicemember was critically injured, to maintain their options to have children.

Whether the new benefit becomes permanent will likely hinge on how the demonstration project affects retention. Beyond tracking cost and participation, the Pentagon has said it wants to understand whether offering the benefit affects how troops and their families view deployments and long separations, a question that goes to the heart of recruitment and retention pressures the services have faced in recent years. For now, the reimbursement applies only for the length of the three-year pilot, though the notice leaves open the possibility that the department could extend it through a subsequent Federal Register notice.

text:
The Defense Health Agency will launch a three-year pilot on Sept. 14, 2026, to support eligible service members who want to freeze sperm or eggs through the Cryopreservation Demonstration Program — 30 days after being listed in the Federal Register.

Mandated by the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025, the demonstration program will reimburse certain costs tied to sperm or egg freezing, giving eligible service members more choice in family planning.

The program, overseen by the DHA medical affairs directorate, “offers support for members who face unique military demands,” said Air Force Maj. (Dr.) Kathleen Pombier, chief of DHA’s women’s health clinical management team. “Military service has an impact on how people build their families, with deployments and long separations affecting when troops decide to have children.”

Cryopreservation safely freezes eggs or sperm with liquid nitrogen to stop the aging process. The frozen eggs and sperm can be thawed, even years later, so service members can use them when the time better fits their family planning objectives, said Pombier.

Designed to give active duty service members “flexibility in choosing when to build their family,” cryopreservation can provide them with more “options in their reproductive future, or if there are issues with getting pregnant,” she said. By providing these family planning possibilities, the program ensures the delivery of high-quality care to all beneficiaries, Pombier added.

In DHA’s effort to deliver joint warfighting capabilities, the pilot covers all active duty forces — U.S. Army, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Air Force, and U.S Space Force. To be eligible, a service member must meet one of three conditions:

Have orders for duty that qualify for hazardous duty pay

Be likely to receive orders for duty that qualify for hazardous duty pay within 120 days

Who will, under orders, be geographically separated from a spouse, domestic partner, or dating partner for more than 180 days, including sea duty

The program is voluntary and not a TRICARE benefit, Pombier noted. Participants can be reimbursed up to $500 per year for sperm preservation and capped at $10,000 per year for egg preservation. The demonstration program will also reimburse for related medications, medical tests, lab work, and imaging. Storage and shipping causes may also be reimbursed. Embryo creation, in vitro fertilization, or other elective procedures are not covered.

“We encourage participants to use a participating military hospital or clinic,” said Pombier, but a civilian fertility clinic may also be used, and doesn’t have to be TRICARE-authorized.

Participants must follow timing guidelines: All testing, retrieval, and freezing generally must occur before orders begin. Beneficiaries who face a qualifying long separation may receive services before the separation or while it continues, if care is available.

Pombier said those interested should begin with the DHA’s program website to get started. All service members must get confirmation of eligibility from their commander before seeking reimbursement. An advance medical directive is also required of all participants stating how they want their stored sperm or eggs handled if they die.

Throughout the demonstration program phase, DHA will track use, costs, claims processing, patient experience, and impact on readiness and retention — all part of a feasibility assessment, Pombier said.

The program is set to end after the initial three-year mandate, unless it’s extended. Pombier said eligible participants should expect to pay storage and shipping costs after the pilot ends if the program doesn’t continue.

text:
MHS Pediatric Vaccine Program Likely to Feel Effects

WASHINGTON, DC — Last month, the Senate confirmed the nomination of Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, JD, a former Navy physician and chief medical officer of the Coast Guard, as director of the national Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) despite fears from both Republicans and Democrats that she will fail to push back against the anti-vaccine agenda of the Trump administration.

During her confirmation hearing, Schwartz assured lawmakers she “will never betray the science,” but fell short of saying she would defy the president or HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Schwartz will be put to the test as, days after her confirmation, President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking to reduce the number of vaccines children receive from 17 to 11 and to separate the single-shot MMR vaccine into five shots requiring five separate visits to the doctor. The order received immediate pushback from lawmakers and health organizations who argued that it went against the best-known science.

“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have expertise to make these changes,” wrote Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA). “Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection. … Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong.”

Cassidy, the chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, oversaw both the confirmation of Schwartz and Kennedy, who has sought to reshape national policy to coincide with his long-standing antivaccine views.

The Department of Health & Human Services announced the following in January:

Recommended for all children are vaccines covering measles, mumps, rubella, polio, pertussis, diphtheria, tetanus, Hib, pneumococcal disease, varicella, and HPV (adjusted to a single HPV dose).

Reserved for high-risk groups, i.e., specific vulnerable populations, are vaccines for RSV, hepatitis A and hepatitis B.

Influenza and COVID-19 may be administered subject to individual doctor-family choice.

Within days, more than half of states announced that they were rejecting some or all of the new guidelines. The American Academy of Pediatrics (APA) and several other public health groups filed a lawsuit against HHS, and in March a federal judge granted preliminary relief, at least temporarily halting the overhaul.

The new executive order is an attempt to reignite that effort.

“Implementation of my administration’s prior directives regarding childhood vaccines has been delayed due to litigation. … Therefore, I am taking further action to reaffirm that it is the policy of the United States that the core childhood vaccine recommendations should be aligned with scientific evidence and best practices from peer, developed countries,” Trump wrote in the order. “States and territories are advised to review the [new recommendations] and consider updating relevant laws and regulations.”

While states set their own regulations on the vaccines required for children to attend public school–—regulations that frequently extend to daycare and private schools—those regulations have historically followed CDC guidance. However, after the attempted overhaul in January, many states said they would be following APA recommendations, which are in line with pre-Trump CDC recommendations.

For military families under TRICARE, the defense healthcare program “covers age-appropriate doses of vaccines as recommended by the CDC,” whether those are received at a military hospital or a civilian provider. With the APA lawsuit still pending, the CDC’s published vaccine schedule still reflects the 2025 recommendations.

How Schwartz will respond in light of the new order has yet to be seen. She is the third person to be nominated as CDC director in the last 18 months. The first, David Weldon, MD, was withdrawn from consideration when it was clear he did not have the votes to be confirmed. The second, Susan Monarez, PhD, was dismissed in August 2025, less than a month after being sworn in. Her dismissal came after she refused an order from Kennedy to approve “every Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommendation, regardless of the scientific evidence” and to fire officials responsible for vaccine policy without cause.

“You can be the CDC director and just take orders. We need a CDC director who will stand up to crazy, stupid things that undermine faith in immunization,” Cassidy told Schwartz during her confirmation hearing. “We’ve got thousands of kids hospitalized because people have promoted that immunization is bad, and now kids have died because of it. It is evil to do that, yet people persist. You are the bulwark. Will you have the ability to stand up to that political meddling?”

Vaccine policy has become one of the few areas where congressional Republicans have publicly disagreed with the president, as the administration’s dismantling of vaccine regulations has coincided with a number of outbreaks. As of August, the CDC had logged 2,465 U.S. measles cases in 2026. That already exceeded the 2,289 logged in 2025. There were 285 confirmed measles cases in 2024.

The administration’s skepticism around vaccines was also seen in the recent decision by DoD to discontinue its mandatory flu vaccine policy. A flu outbreak among new recruits at Lackland Air Force Base that resulted in one death prompted services to reinstate the vaccine for basic trainees.

text:
An executive order signed Sept. 8 by President Donald Trump would require the Pentagon and the VA to tackle two long-standing issues facing those about to leave service – the handoff of personnel records between the departments and improved access to employment opportunities.

The order imposes a timeline on improvements addressing both issues. For records:

Within 30 days, the Pentagon and the VA are to “ensure all current service member Official Military Personnel Files, health records, and Service Treatment Records are shared” between the agencies after the member leaves uniform.

Within 120 days, federal officials must review all software systems connected to the order for compatibility with military records, and ensure future systems remain compatible.

Within 180 days, the record-sharing established at the 30-day mark must be “permanent, prospective, and ongoing … from the moment an individual enters into military service until such time as he or she no longer requires benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs.”

“Giving VA continuous access to warfighters’ military records will eliminate weeks of waiting for veterans applying for VA health care and financial benefits,” VA secretary Doug Collins said in a press release announcing the order. “We want to make the transition from military to Veteran status as seamless as possible, and we look forward to working with President Trump and Department of War Secretary Pete Hegseth to do just that.”

Transition-related improvements also come with a timeline, as changes to streamline access to benefits and updates to the Transition Assistance Program are due in 180 days. Updates require coordination between the Pentagon, the VA, and the Labor Department to connect veterans with “specific, open jobs in fields related to their skills [and] interests,” enroll them in Labor Department-funded job training, or connect them with a veterans representative to assist in applying for education, disability, health care, or other service-earned benefits.

[RELATED: Transition and Career Assistance From MOAA]

MOAA looks forward to working with the VA and other stakeholders to support the association’s goals of an improved Pentagon-VA records handoff and expanded access to proven, results-oriented transition and career support.

text:
SEPTEMBER 9, 2026 – When you have a medical appointment on the calendar, it’s best to prepare ahead of time. It doesn’t take long, and the benefits will help you make the most of your healthcare appointment.

“It’s important to be familiar with what your TRICARE plan covers. You should have all the necessary documents available and be ready with questions for your provider before you go to your appointment,” said Dr. Ross Colt, Medical Director, Clinical Oversight and Integration, TRICARE Health Plan, at the Defense Health Agency. “Whether you’re meeting with a primary care provider or specialist, being prepared can help streamline the check-in process and maximize your time with your provider.”

Depending on where you’re getting care, check out these guidelines so you’re ready for your upcoming appointment.

If you have an appointment at a military hospital or clinic

Your military hospital or clinic will have your electronic health record through your MHS GENESIS Patient Portal. However, every time you see your provider, be sure to:

Bring your Uniformed Services ID card

Make notes to discuss with your provider, including any symptoms (with a timeline, if possible), questions, or concerns you have

Have ready a list of allergies, immunizations, over-the-counter supplements, and any lifestyle changes since your last appointment

Did you know that military hospitals and clinics worldwide have a chaperone policy? The policy states that you or your provider can request a trained chaperone to be present in the exam room for any type of exam, including dental exams. Chaperones are a part of the clinical team—they’re a safeguard for both patients and staff.

If you’re seeing a civilian provider

If you’re meeting with a civilian doctor, make sure you know if your provider is a TRICARE network or non-network provider. To limit your out-of-pocket costs, verify that your TRICARE plan covers the services you’re receiving.

Double check you’re carrying your Uniformed Services ID card, other health insurance card (if you have OHI), and any required copayment or cost-share.

Additionally, bring a comprehensive list of your:

Family’s medical history

Personal medical conditions of note, particularly those regarding illness, hospitalization, or surgery

Current medications, including vitamins, supplements, and herbal remedies

Allergies, especially medications

Immunization and vaccine records

If you’re meeting with a specialist

Your plan determines if you need a referral to see specialist providers. Active duty service members need referrals for any care their primary care manager doesn’t provide. Beneficiaries enrolled in a TRICARE Prime plan need referrals for most care their primary care manager doesn’t provide. In these cases, your PCM will refer you to another provider or a specialist.

Those enrolled in all other TRICARE plans only need pre-authorization for certain services.

If you have Medicare and TRICARE For Life

As described in the Medicare and You Handbook, you’ll need to bring all your health insurance cards with you to your appointment. If you have original Medicare, bring your red, white, and blue Medicare card and your Uniformed Services ID card to your appointment.

If you’re enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan or have OHI, be sure to bring the plan ID cards, as well as your Uniformed Services ID card.

If any of your insurance coverages have changed, be sure to inform your provider’s office to ensure your claims are processed appropriately.

Other general reminders

Gather your medical information: Be as thorough, thoughtful, and honest as possible with your family history and personal health status.

Prepare for the type of visit scheduled.

Are you going for an annual physical or preventive or diagnostic screening? Ask ahead of time if there are any special guidelines for your visit, such as fasting for bloodwork or arriving with a full bladder for an ultrasound.

Are you ill, have symptoms, and seeking treatment? It’s helpful if you’ve tracked your symptoms. Know what your symptoms are and when they started. This helps your provider identify what you have and how best to treat you.

Do you have questions for your provider? Make a comprehensive list to get the answers you need. You may want to take notes during your discussion.

Keep in mind, there isn’t a TRICARE card to show your provider as proof of eligibility. Learn more about what identification you need to bring with you to your appointment. And remember to check your information in the Defense Eligibility and Enrollment Reporting System and make any necessary updates. Avoid claims, billings, authorizations, and other issues by keeping your DEERS account current.

Taking some time to prepare for your appointment helps ensure a more meaningful and productive appointment with your provider.

text:
HOUSTON — Pancreatic cancer is recognized by the VA as a presumptive service-connected condition linked to toxic burn pit exposure under the PACT Act.

According to the National Institutes of Health and the American Cancer Society, about 67,000 cases of pancreatic cancer are diagnosed annually, with veterans facing a higher incidence than non-veterans. Last year, a new program at the Michael E. DeBakey VAMC was designated by the National Pancreas Foundation (NPF) as the first Center of Excellence for pancreas care within the VA system.

Now, a new treatment option for pancreatic cancer is creating optimism about improving survival for the deadly disease at the VA and elsewhere.

In late August, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved daraxonrasib, marketed as Rasonque, a RAS inhibitor for the most common form of pancreatic cancer. Rasonque, a tablet taken once daily, targets multiple forms of a protein called RAS, a key driver of tumor growth in most patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, which arises from cells lining the ducts of the pancreas. The approval was granted to Revolution Medicines, Inc. in Redwood City, CA.

“Today’s approval provides a critical new option for patients facing an extraordinarily difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer. It is our fundamental duty to deliver more cures and meaningful treatments to patients as quickly as possible,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, JD. The approval is for the treatment of adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who have received at least one prior systemic therapy or are not candidates for multiagent systemic therapy.

Approximately 90% to 95% of the 67,000 new cases of pancreatic cancer diagnosed in the United States each year are pancreatic adenocarcinoma, according to the National Cancer Institute. Even though it represents only about 3.2% of all cancer diagnoses, pancreatic adenocarcinoma accounts for a disproportionately high share of cancer deaths. The reasons range from typically late detection, aggressive disease course and historically limited treatment options.

In a randomized, open-label, multicenter clinical trial involving 500 adults with previously treated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, Rasonque improved median overall survival to 13.2 months compared to 6.7 months for standard chemotherapy. In the Phase 3 RASolute 302 trial, RASONQUE reduced the risk of death by 60% and demonstrated an unprecedented overall survival benefit compared with chemotherapy, with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements across all primary and key secondary endpoints.1

On Sept. 8 at approximately 2:35 p.m., members of the Pleasantville Fire Department responded to a structure fire off the 700 block of New Jersey Avenue.

Four residents were displaced, and one firefighter sustained a minor injury, officials said.

No residents were injured in the fire, and all occupants were accounted for prior to firefighting operations, members of the department said in a press release.

According to a press release, preliminary reports from dispatch indicated an explosion was heard prior to the crews' arrival. The structure was already under heavy fire conditions when firefighters arrived.

Crews made an interior attack on the fire, but as structural conditions deteriorated, firefighters shifted extinguishing attempts to a defensive, exterior strategy.

Fire officials posted on Facebook that operations shifted to protect surrounding structures as conditions on the scene changed.

The four displaced residents were assisted by the American Red Cross. The injured firefighter did not require EMS treatment.

Members of Tricare Medical Transportation and the Pleasantville Police Department assisted fire crews on the scene. Battalion 1 was the duty shift at the time of the incident, and mutual aid was provided by multiple departments across South Jersey.

The cause of the fire, including the reported explosion, remains under investigation by members of the Pleasantville Fire Department.

title: Active Surveillance Chosen by 93% of Veterans With Low-Risk Prostate Cancer
description:
In 2024, 93% of veterans with low-risk prostate cancer chose active surveillance or monitoring the tumor with regular testing rather than treating it right away compared with just 27% in 2005.
Of those, 38,130 were managed initially with active surveillance, also called watchful waiting, at a median age of 65.
Active surveillance typically involves blood tests for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) every three to six months, along with less frequent digital rectal exams, MRI, and repeat biopsies.
I sometimes highlight the word ‘active’ in active surveillance, to reassure patients that we are keeping a very close eye with measured steps and not just forgetting about the diagnosis.” The message seems to be getting through.
“A surveillance approach is more likely in the VA system than in outside clinical practices,” said Lee.
text:
SAN FRANCISCO — Three decades after the VA and the University of California-San Francisco helped pioneer active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer, the strategy has become the default choice for veterans diagnosed with the disease, according to a study published Aug. 13 in JAMA. In 2024, 93% of veterans with low-risk prostate cancer chose active surveillance or monitoring the tumor with regular testing rather than treating it right away compared with just 27% in 2005. Among veterans with favorable intermediate-risk disease, active surveillance use rose to 61% in 2024 from 14% in 2005.1

Researchers from UCSF and the San Francisco VA Health Care System, working with the VA’s PROFOUND-VET initiative and VA Boston Healthcare System, followed more than 73,000 veterans diagnosed with low-risk or favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer across the VA system between 2005 and 2024. Of those, 38,130 were managed initially with active surveillance, also called watchful waiting, at a median age of 65.

Active surveillance typically involves blood tests for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) every three to six months, along with less frequent digital rectal exams, MRI, and repeat biopsies. Surgery or radiation is considered only if the disease shows signs of progressing. The approach has been shown to produce survival outcomes on par with immediate treatment while avoiding the risk of urinary incontinence, bowel issues, and erectile dysfunction associated with surgery and radiation.

“Prostate cancer screening saves thousands of lives by finding aggressive cancers early, but it also detects many slow-growing cancers that do not spread, and should not be treated except in rare situations,” said senior author Matthew Cooperberg, MD, MPH, chief of urology at the San Francisco VAMC and co-director of the Prostate Program at the UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. “Many experts are recommending that we not even call these ‘cancers,’” he added. “Patients with early disease who say they prefer treatment may need better counseling.”

Using the word ‘cancer’ for these cases creates anxiety and leads many patients to reflexively seek treatment, but education can temper that reaction.

“We counsel our patients on the known nature of low-risk disease, notably that Gleason grade (GG) group 1 prostate cancer is effectively incapable of metastasizing,” first author Grace Lee, MD, a fifth-year urology resident at UCSF who also practices at the San Francisco VA told U.S. Medicine. “We discuss how this disease can be safely monitored with an individualized schedule that includes PSA, MRI, and repeat prostate biopsy. I sometimes highlight the word ‘active’ in active surveillance, to reassure patients that we are keeping a very close eye with measured steps and not just forgetting about the diagnosis.”

The message seems to be getting through. The study found that tumor grade, rather than PSA level, was the stronger driver of whether patients pursued surveillance in keeping with current guidelines. Among patients whose intermediate-risk classification was based on a PSA under 10 ng/mL with a small proportion of biopsy cores showing higher-grade disease, surveillance use rose from 11% to 55% over the study period; among those with lower-grade disease but a higher PSA, it rose from 27% to 88%.

Surveillance rates varied by facility, ranging from 23% to 93% overall, though for low-risk patients diagnosed since 2015, all but one VA site used surveillance in at least 60% of cases.

In statistical models adjusting for other factors, older age and more recent year of diagnosis were both associated with higher odds of active surveillance, while Black and Hispanic patients, and veterans living in more disadvantaged areas, had somewhat lower odds independent of their cancer’s clinical features, a gap the study’s authors flagged as warranting further attention. Distance a veteran had to travel to a VA facility was not associated with surveillance use.

“A surveillance approach is more likely in the VA system than in outside clinical practices,” said Lee. “The VA is an integrated healthcare system that has robust practices for tracking quality of care and providing feedback to physicians, and facilitates long-term continuity of patient care.”

The findings build on a long history of VA-driven prostate cancer research. The Gleason score, the grading system used almost universally today to gauge how aggressive a prostate tumor is likely to be, was developed in the 1960s by pathologist Donald Gleason at the Minneapolis VA Health Care System.

The study continues the groundbreaking work by the VA in prostate cancer, notably the development of the Gleason score in the 1960s by Donald Gleason at the Minneapolis VA Health Care System and the landmark PIVOT trial that randomized men with localized prostate cancer to either surgery or observation and followed them for nearly two decades. Published in 2017, it found that surgery was not associated with significantly lower all-cause or prostate-cancer-specific mortality than observation, while carrying a higher rate of adverse events. Surgery was associated with less treatment of disease progression, most of which was asymptomatic or biochemical rather than clinical or life-threatening.2

Taken together, the authors of the new study concluded, the findings suggest that nearly all veterans with favorable-risk prostate cancer receive care that matches national guidelines. That’s substantially better than results in the general population. Less than 60% of men diagnosed with low-risk prostate cancer in the U.S. are managed with active surveillance, a previous study led by Cooperberg found.3 While the general trend showed a steady rise, the study found that some urology practices managed no patients with low-risk disease with watchful waiting.

Further, the study demonstrates the system-wide adoption of staged screening and conservative care.

“A high PSA by no means diagnoses a clinically threatening prostate cancer, but it does tell the roughly 75% of the population with PSA <1 at midlife that their risk of lethal prostate cancer ever is incredibly low,” Cooperberg told U.S. Medicine. “If the PSA is higher then we have a wide range of blood, urine, and imaging tests that should be used next, followed by a biopsy only if indicated by those secondary tests. And then we need to be clear that we should only treat if we find potentially lethal disease, meaning at least a substantial GG2.”

title: TRICARE's Autism Care Demonstration: How Military Families Get ABA Therapy Approved
description:
Active duty families must also register their child in the Extended Care Health Option, the echo program TRICARE requires before ACD participation begins.
What the ECHO Program TRICARE Requires Before ABA Starts ECHO is a supplemental benefit for beneficiaries with qualifying conditions, and autism spectrum disorder is explicitly on that list.
Does TRICARE Cover ABA Therapy, and What Do TRICARE Autism Benefits Cost?
Frequently Asked Questions What is the ECHO program TRICARE requires for ABA therapy?
How long does a TRICARE ABA authorization last?
text:
Every military family raising an autistic child eventually hits the same wall. A diagnosis is in hand, the pediatrician agrees therapy makes sense, and then nothing moves for months. The obstacle is rarely clinical. It is paperwork, and it has a specific shape.

Here is the short version. ABA therapy for military families is covered through the Comprehensive Autism Care Demonstration, a benefit that sits separate from standard TRICARE medical coverage. Active duty families must also register their child in the Extended Care Health Option, the echo program TRICARE requires before ACD participation begins. The approval path runs in order: get an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis from an approved provider, obtain a referral and pre-authorization, complete four baseline outcome measures, then begin services under a six-month authorization that renews. The demonstration began in 2014 and is authorized through 2028. Understanding that sequence is the difference between waiting three months and waiting nine, and it is the same sequence behind every in-home and school-based ABA program Apex ABA runs across North Carolina, Georgia, and Maryland.

What the ECHO Program TRICARE Requires Before ABA Starts

ECHO is a supplemental benefit for beneficiaries with qualifying conditions, and autism spectrum disorder is explicitly on that list. For active duty families it is not optional. Service members with a child diagnosed with ASD must enroll in their branch's Exceptional Family Member Program, and the child must also register for ECHO.

Three details cost families the most time:

Registration is not retroactive. TRICARE is direct about this: there is no retroactive registration for ECHO. Time spent waiting is not recovered later.

The condition must be entered correctly in DEERS. If the disability is not properly recorded in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System, ECHO services are not accessible, regardless of what the diagnosis paperwork says.

There is a provisional window. In the East Region, a child can begin using ECHO services during a 90-day provisional period while registration is completed. Families who know this do not sit and wait for a final confirmation letter.

EFMP enrollment can be waived in limited situations, such as when the branch does not operate an EFMP or when the child lives with a custodial parent who is not the active duty sponsor. Retirees and their families are eligible for the ACD without ECHO, since ECHO eligibility is tied to active duty, activated Guard and Reserve, and certain transitional categories.

TRICARE East ABA: Who Approves the Request, and the Five Steps It Runs Through

North Carolina, Georgia, and Maryland all sit in the TRICARE East Region, where Humana Military is the current regional contractor. Every TRICARE East ABA authorization letter, reauthorization, and provider assignment moves through that contractor. West Region families work with TriWest Healthcare Alliance instead. Knowing which entity holds the file matters, because that is who to call when an authorization stalls.

One correction worth making early: the referral comes from the diagnosing provider, not from the ABA agency. Families often contact a clinic first and lose weeks discovering the referral was never submitted.

The five steps run like this:

Diagnosis from an approved provider. That means a primary care provider in family practice, pediatrics, or a pediatric or family nurse practitioner role, or a board-certified or board-eligible specialist such as a doctoral-level clinical psychologist, developmental behavioral pediatrician, neurodevelopmental pediatrician, pediatric neurologist, or child psychiatrist. The diagnosis carries the F84.0 code that appears on every claim afterward.

Referral and pre-authorization. Every TRICARE plan requires both. The diagnosing provider sends a referral to the regional contractor, which issues an authorization letter. First-time families receive an initial letter covering the ABA assessment, then a second covering six months of services once the treatment plan is written.

Four baseline outcome measures. Before services begin, the family and provider team complete the Pervasive Developmental Disorder Behavior Inventory, the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, the Social Responsiveness Scale, and either the Parenting Stress Index or the Stress Index for Parents of Adolescents, depending on the child's age.

Services start. If care is not offered within the 28-day specialty care access standard, or the family wants a different provider, the regional contractor can be contacted directly. Many families move to in-home ABA sessions at this stage because it removes commute time from an already compressed schedule.

The Autism Services Navigator. TRICARE assigns an ASN as primary care coordinator, and families assigned one must complete a comprehensive care plan within 90 days. Beneficiaries in the US Family Health Plan or living overseas do not receive an ASN.

Does TRICARE Cover ABA Therapy, and What Do TRICARE Autism Benefits Cost?

Yes, with conditions, and the cost structure is more generous than most commercial plans.

Families pay the standard copayment or cost-share for their TRICARE plan. All ABA services delivered on a single day are subject to one copayment, and those amounts apply toward the calendar year catastrophic cap. ECHO itself carries a separate monthly cost-share tied to pay grade, charged only in months the benefit is used.

One point deserves emphasis. TRICARE places no yearly or lifetime caps on the amount of ABA it covers. A child will not hit a benefit maximum and be cut off mid-year. That contrasts sharply with state-regulated commercial plans, where hard annual dollar caps in North Carolina and elsewhere are routine.

The other cost is administrative, and three clocks run at once:

Every six months: the ASN updates the comprehensive care plan, the provider completes the applicable outcome measures, and the contractor authorizes the next treatment period.

Every twelve months: additional outcome measures come due.

Every twenty-four months: a new referral and DSM-5 checklist documentation are required from the diagnosing provider.

That twenty-four-month referral is the one families forget, because it falls outside the rhythm of everything else. It does not arrive with a reminder from the contractor, it does not line up with the six-month reauthorization the ABA provider handles, and it requires a return visit to the diagnosing provider rather than a form the therapy team can submit. Marking the date on a household calendar the week the first authorization arrives costs nothing and prevents a lapse two years out.

What ABA Therapy TRICARE Approval Looks Like in Practice

Consider a composite scenario drawn from cases our team sees regularly. An active duty Army family stationed near Fort Meade has a four-year-old recently diagnosed by a developmental behavioral pediatrician. The parents assume the diagnosis is the finish line. It is the starting line.

Their actual sequence: EFMP enrollment through the sponsor's branch, ECHO registration with the condition confirmed in DEERS, then a referral submitted by the diagnosing pediatrician to Humana Military. An authorization letter arrives covering the ABA assessment. A BCBA completes the assessment and writes the treatment plan. The family completes the four outcome measures. A second authorization letter covers six months of services. An ASN is assigned, and the comprehensive care plan is finalized inside the 90-day window.

Families who run these steps in parallel rather than sequentially, particularly starting ECHO registration the same day the diagnosis is confirmed, consistently shorten the gap. Apex ABA works with Maryland families at exactly this stage and can often identify the missing document before another cycle closes.

Relocation is where authorizations most often break. Before orders take effect, contact both the child's case manager and the regional contractor, and ask three things: where the current six-month authorization expires, whether the most recent outcome measures are current and on file, and whether the receiving location actually has board certified behavior analysts in network. Coverage of a duty station does not guarantee local provider capacity. Families sometimes ask a related question about the other direction, whether an autistic young adult can serve, which turns on a separate set of enlistment and waiver rules.

What the 2025 National Academies Review Means for TRICARE Autism Benefits

In October 2025, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine published a congressionally mandated independent analysis of the ACD. The committee included Brian Boyd, PhD, and Sam Odom, PhD, both Frank Porter Graham researchers at the University of North Carolina.

The findings explain why the process feels heavier than it does for civilian families:

Roughly 16,000 TRICARE-eligible beneficiaries are currently enrolled in the ACD.

Across 2018 to 2023, 109,073 TRICARE-eligible children ages 1 to 18 had an autism diagnosis. Of those, 35,034, or 32 percent, had a claim for ABA services.

Among children who did receive ABA, 60 percent received fewer than five hours per week. Twenty or more hours per week was rare, at 4 percent.

The committee concluded that military-connected families face greater burdens to maintain eligibility than civilian families face under comparable plans, and that some providers have limited or ended TRICARE participation as a result.

The central recommendation was to end the demonstration and authorize ABA as a standard TRICARE Basic benefit. That has not happened yet, so the requirements above remain in force. The report also found that autism prevalence among military families may run slightly higher than the general population, roughly 3.5 to 4.5 percent against a CDC general-population estimate of 1 in 31 eight-year-olds, while cautioning that those figures come from studies using different methods and are not directly comparable.

Paperwork should never be the reason a child waits. If your family is somewhere between the diagnosis and the authorization letter, tell us exactly where things stalled. Our intake team works ACD requirements every week across North Carolina, Georgia, and Maryland, and we can usually spot the missing document before another six-month window closes. Send us a note and let's untangle it together.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ECHO program TRICARE requires for ABA therapy?

ECHO is the Extended Care Health Option, a supplemental TRICARE benefit for beneficiaries with qualifying conditions including autism. Active duty family members must be registered in ECHO to participate in the Autism Care Demonstration.

Does TRICARE cover ABA therapy?

Yes, through the Comprehensive Autism Care Demonstration rather than the standard medical benefit. Coverage requires an approved ASD diagnosis, a referral, and pre-authorization.

How long does a TRICARE ABA authorization last?

Six months. Your provider submits a reauthorization request with an updated treatment plan and outcome measures before each period ends.

How often do I need a new referral for ABA under TRICARE?

Every twenty-four months. Your PCM or ASD diagnosing provider must submit a new referral and DSM-5 checklist documentation.

Do retirees need ECHO to get ABA through TRICARE?

No. ECHO registration applies to active duty family members. Retirees and their qualifying family members can access the ACD without it.

Is ABA covered under TRICARE overseas?

Only in a small number of overseas locations, and generally only under the sole provider model delivered by board certified behavior analysts. Tiered ABA is not authorized overseas except in US territories.

title: Obesity Medications Can Reduce Muscle and Bone Health in Older Adults - U.S. Medicine
description:
The review article published in Obesity examined age-associated changes in muscle and bone in older adults prescribed incretin mimetic therapies, which are highly effective medications used in the treatment of overweight and obesity, which occur in about 40% of older adults.
The authors suggested that the use of incretin mimetics in older adults to treat overweight and obesity is expected to rise, because these medications result in significant weight reduction and improvements in cardiovascular health and quality of life.
Older adults experience accelerated losses in skeletal muscle mass and bone mineral density, however, and it’s unclear how incretin mimetics affect these processes.
The paper is not suggesting clinicians avoid GLP-1-based therapies in older adults, but it does highlight that we should prescribe very thoughtfully, paying attention to preserving muscle and bone health.
“Recent evidence outside of this review is reassuring that these therapies remain effective in older adults,” Shoemaker said.
text:
CHAPEL HILL, NC — As prescribing increases for obesity medications, such as glucagon-likepeptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (also called incretin mimetics), the magnitude of the effects of these therapies on lean soft tissue, physical function and fragility fracture in older adults remains unclear, according to a recent review.

The review article published in Obesity examined age-associated changes in muscle and bone in older adults prescribed incretin mimetic therapies, which are highly effective medications used in the treatment of overweight and obesity, which occur in about 40% of older adults. The analysis also explored current evidence on the effects and associations of incretin mimetics on physical function and fragility fracture risk in older adults.1

The study was led by the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston, TX, and included participation from the Durham, NC, VAMC.

The authors suggested that the use of incretin mimetics in older adults to treat overweight and obesity is expected to rise, because these medications result in significant weight reduction and improvements in cardiovascular health and quality of life. Older adults experience accelerated losses in skeletal muscle mass and bone mineral density, however, and it’s unclear how incretin mimetics affect these processes.

“Considering a rising trend in the prescription of incretin mimetics to treat obesity in older adulthood, a more robust characterization of the impact of these medications on lean soft tissue, physical function and fragility fracture is needed to support future clinical decision making in older adults with overweight/obesity,” the researchers wrote.

In this review, the study authors identified several incretin mimetic weight reduction trials that demonstrated significant losses in lean soft tissue (six studies) and/or indices of bone (three studies). Still, they noted the clinical significance of these decreases on physical function and/or fragility fracture remains unclear.

The investigators determined that losses in muscle-based indices (e.g., lean soft tissue) following incretin mimetic therapy are common, accounting for as much as 40% of total weight reduction in some randomized controlled trials. They also found limited data that suggest that significant decreases in central site (e.g., hip, lumbar spine) bone mineral density might be a consequence of incretin mimetic therapy.

Overall, the researchers concluded that the magnitude of the effects of incretin mimetic therapies in older adults is unclear, and the influence of these therapies on physical function and fragility fracture risk are poorly described. Because of the growing trend to prescribe incretin mimetics to treat obesity in older adults, the authors suggested that a more detailed description of how incretin mimetics influence changes in body composition and whether these changes contribute to physical dysfunction and/or fragility fracture in older adults is needed to support future clinical decision-making in overweight or obese adults.

“The review highlights some important information: bone and muscle loss does occur as we age, and it is well known that non-fat loss occurs with any type of weight loss,” Melissa Shoemaker, MD, MPH, a spokesperson for The Obesity Society, told U.S. Medicine. “So we should always be encouraging patients of all ages to be as physically active as possible and eat balanced nutrition. The paper is not suggesting clinicians avoid GLP-1-based therapies in older adults, but it does highlight that we should prescribe very thoughtfully, paying attention to preserving muscle and bone health. Prior to starting treatment, clinicians should assess factors such as frailty, fall risk, osteoporosis, nutritional status and baseline physical functioning.”

During treatment, Shoemaker recommended that clinicians should ask not only how much weight a patient has lost but also whether the patient is maintaining strength, mobility and adequate nutrition. Resistance exercise should be prescribed as a patient is able, along with sufficient protein, calcium, vitamin D and overall energy intake.

In addition, clinicians should utilize referrals to physical therapists, exercise physiologists and registered dietitians as needed to help reduce barriers and encourage consistency. Appetite suppression also can be profound with these medications, so clinicians should actively monitor for patients who are eating too little, underconsuming protein or experiencing severe or persistent gastrointestinal symptoms, Shoemaker pointed out.

The study authors also advised that decreases in lean mass should be interpreted carefully. Lean mass measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) doesn’t always equate to functional skeletal muscle, and current evidence hasn’t consistently shown that lean mass lost during incretin therapy translates into clinically meaningful weakness, disability or fractures.

In fact, the few studies referenced that included physical functioning seemed to show a benefit, Shoemaker noted, which is similar to what she sees clinically and what has been learned from bariatric surgery, where patients lose lean mass during substantial weight loss but often experience improvements in mobility and independence.

For clinicians caring for veterans, military personnel and American Indian/Alaska Native populations, which are groups with disproportionately high rates of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease, the potential benefits of these medications are substantial and should certainly be considered, Shoemaker explained.

“Recent evidence outside of this review is reassuring that these therapies remain effective in older adults,” Shoemaker said. “A recent meta-analysis of older adults found that GLP-1-based medications significantly reduced major adverse cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death and kidney outcomes, with benefits comparable to those seen in younger adults and extending even to patients aged 75 years and older. Likewise, recent analyses of tirzepatide have demonstrated similar efficacy and safety in older versus younger adults.”

“I don’t think the message is that older adults should not receive these medications, but they should be used with additional monitoring,” Shoemaker suggested. “The goal should be to individualize therapy based on a patient’s overall health, functional status and goals of care, while also incorporating strategies that help preserve muscle strength, bone health, and long-term independence and quality of life.”

In the future, the authors recommended that randomized controlled trials and real-world observational studies are needed to clearly explain the relationship between incretin mimetics and body composition in older adult populations and to evaluate approaches (e.g., life-style modification) that lessen decreases in skeletal muscle mass and bone during incretin mimetic therapy for obesity.

PRESS RELEASE

Published September 8, 2026

TSC and ITG continue their multi year partnership and win SEWP VI

Technology Science Corporation (TSC) and Integration Technologies Group, Inc. (ITG) have been awarded a NASA Solutions for Enterprise-wide Procurement - SEWP VI contract under Category C, the companies announced, extending a partnership between the two firms that stretches back more than a decade. The award was made to TSC-ITG2 JV LLC (https://tsc-itg2.com/), an SBA-approved mentor-protégé joint venture between the two firms.

SEWP VI remains the government's flagship vehicle for acquiring information and communications technology, structured as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract worth up to $20 billion over a ten-year ordering period running November 1, 2026 through October 31, 2036. Category C is reserved for IT mission-based services, and under the award, TSC-ITG2 JV LLC will support complex, end-to-end IT services and digital transformation programs for federal agencies.

The win formalizes a relationship years in the making. TSC (https://www.techscicorp.com/) and ITG (https://www.itgonline.com/) first began working together in 2015, collaborating on a series of professional services projects before establishing their initial SBA-approved joint venture, TSC-ITG JV LLC, in 2020. A second joint venture followed in 2025. Over that stretch, the two companies have jointly supported Federal, Civilian, and DoW for more than ten years on professional, maintenance, and lifecycle services work overseas through GSA MAS, GSA Stars 3 and agency-specific IDIQ.

For ITG, the award builds directly on its record under SEWP V, where the company held a prime contract (NNG15SC79B) and delivered hundreds of task orders in hardware, software, and services to agencies including the Defense Logistics Agency, the Defense Health Agency, the Defense Finance and Accounting Service, the Air Force, and NASA - work that consistently earned strong performance ratings. Through TSC-ITG2 JV LLC, that track record now extends into IT mission-based services, broadening the portfolio the two companies can offer under a single vehicle.

The joint venture draws on a combined certification and clearance profile the companies describe as among the deepest in the mid-tier federal IT space. TSC brings Top Secret clearance readiness to support mission-critical work across defense and civilian agencies, while ITG contributes CMMC Level 2 (Final) certification with dedicated enclaves for controlled information, CMMI-DEV and CMMI-SVC appraisals, ISO/IEC 27001 and 20000-1 certifications, O-TTPS supply chain certification, and a GSA-audited cybersecurity supply chain risk management plan. Both companies hold ISO 9001 quality management certification. Together, the credentials are intended to give federal customers ordering under SEWP VI confidence in an audited quality system, a certified security posture, and a supply chain protected against counterfeit or compromised components.

TSC-ITG2 JV LLC pairs TSC, a Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned and Woman-Owned Small Business serving as managing partner, with ITG as mentoring partner - a structure designed to combine TSC's agility and clearances with ITG's certified delivery infrastructure and past performance. ITG, founded in 1984, is a Falls Church, Virginia-based provider of IT products, enterprise services, and lifecycle support to federal, state, and commercial customers, with a portfolio that extends into video-teleconferencing systems, accessibility solutions for the visually impaired, post-OEM warranty and maintenance services, and RFID solutions.
