text:
Republican congressional candidate Marty Young has been working with the Chester County physicians to try to stop proposed changes to Medicare that he believes hurt patients and doctors.

In a healthcare policy brief, Young writes that Congress is running out of time to stop changes to Medicare that would require a second visit if a doctor, say a dermatologist, finds a suspicious spot that needs to be removed.

“There’s some urgency about fixing the CMS [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services],” Young said in a recent interview. And Congress needs to fix it. Because if people have a diagnosis and they’ve got to come back a month or two later to get a suspicious mole removed, that’s not good.”

Young, who is running in Pennsylvania’s 6th congressional district, has suggested that the military’s TRICARE program would save money and offer better services, improving healthcare for civilians, in his Young America Healthcare Plan. Previously, Young said his YAHP could serve children and young people to age 23 and pregnant women. Now he’s offering it as a solution to Medicare issues, as well.

“TRICARE is not just optimized on saving taxpayers money,” said Young. “But also optimized around making sure that service members and their families get back to their duties or their daily life. And so I look at the CMS change as being pretty important because it just exposes the fact that Congress passed a really good law in terms of Chapter 55 of Title 10, which created and maintained high morale, right? It improved the medical and dental care. And good morale means if you go to your doctor and your doctor finds something, the doctor can fix it. The doctor fixes it then and there.”

The change in Medicare law is a problem because the patient has to come back again, perhaps travel a distance, pay again, and meanwhile the medical problem, perhaps cancer, could spread.

“You increase the cost in terms of potential outcomes,” said Young.

“And the only real winners are the big healthcare insurance companies,” he said. And those insurers are donors to his opponent, incumbent Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Chester/Berks), he said.

“The real winners are the healthcare insurers, not the local practitioners, not the doctors able to provide that first line of care. It’s a problem,” said Young.

“The big healthcare insurance companies, at the end of the day, are a cost-plus model. So more cost equals more profit. That’s why they like it.”

Young noted that Houlahan has received political contributions from health insurers’ political action committees (PACs).

These include for the 2023-24 cycle, $7,500 from United Healthcare PAC and $2,500 from that PAC in 2025; $5,000 from Humana PAC for the 2023-2024; and $5,000 from Cigna PAC for 2023-24.

Main Line Dermatology sent a letter asking its patients to contact their

congress members and U.S. Senators John Fetterman and David McCormick over proposed changes to Medicare that would lead to an additional trip to the doctor’s office; additional co-pays and out-of-pocket expenses; more time away from work for caregivers; longer waits to receive a diagnosis and begin treatment; greater hardship for patients who travel long distances to see their doctors; and additional medical expenses.

“Ultimately, this decision does not only jeopardize Medicare patients. If this policy goes into effect, other insurance carriers will undoubtedly follow suit. This will mean they are keeping more of your healthcare dollars for their executives and shareholders while providing fewer payments for your care.”

And the issue extends beyond dermatology, the letter added. It would also influence primary care and other specialists who perform office procedures

Houlahan sent this response to Broad + Liberty: “I have heard from many constituents who received an email from Main Line Dermatology. My team and I were already reviewing the proposed 2027 changes, and we reached out to the provider to better understand their specific concerns. In fact, we speak regularly to providers to understand and work to address the inefficiencies and obstacles they face, in this case with the Trump administration’s changes to Medicare. We also work with thousands of our constituents on cases involving Medicare day in and day out. I’m happy to see my opponent agrees that the fee schedule changes are unhelpful and nonsensical.”

Houlahan said she is having her annual Medicare Town Hall Sept.10.

“For the fourth consecutive year, I am hosting state and federal experts to discuss this proposed fee schedule change and many other elements of Medicare coverage across multiple specialties for the coming year. I also highlighted this issue in my September 4 newsletter and alerted constituents that the public comment period for the proposed changes is open until September 14.” If adopted, these changes would take place Jan. 1, 2027.

Houlahan urges everyone to “share their concerns with CMS.”

The Chester County Medical Society invited both Young and Houlahan to discuss healthcare law and regulation. Young answered their questions, but Houlahan’s campaign sent them this response:

“Chrissy Houlahan’s voting record is available on her official website, along with press releases, her social media accounts, and her newsletters. With that in mind, her campaign team have made the decision to not participate in questionnaires on any topic

in this cycle. Please access Chrissy’s priorities and accomplishments on her website: houlahan.house.gov.”

“Independent physicians in Chester County asked for a serious conversation about the payment and regulatory rules closing their practices,” Young said. “One candidate engaged. The other pointed to a website.”

“Healthcare now consumes roughly 18 percent of GDP. Independent practices continue to disappear,” said Young. “And when official debt is combined with unfunded Social Security and Medicare obligations, the United States faces more than $100 trillion in long-term liabilities — costs that fall on families through higher taxes, higher prices and reduced access to local care.”

Young added, “That’s why TRICARE is the right solution as a reforming mechanism,” said Young. On competition between health insurers, he added, “Let them build a better mousetrap.”

text:
To a cohort of emerging military healthcare leaders at the 2026 Tri-Service Chapters Annual Scientific Meeting, Defense Health Agency Director Navy Vice Adm. Darin K. Via positioned the agency as a source of “problem solvers and solution providers” to optimize combat support in generating and sustaining global warfighter readiness.

In his remarks at the meeting in Bethesda, Maryland, Aug. 26, Via called upon future leaders across the military healthcare enterprise to own risk, solve problems at the right level, and focus on ensuring service members are medically ready for the future fight.

“Military medicine faces a more complex future than it did during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan,” Via said. “The enemy has changed the tactics on us, and we have to adapt,” in delivering care to warfighters.

The joint medical education conference is hosted by the American College of Physicians for military internal medicine professionals, including physicians, residents, fellows, and other healthcare professionals.

Via said since the first day he became director of the agency, his goal was to make “the entire DHA a combat support agency.”

His viewpoint shapes how DHA leaders will measure success, Via said, emphasizing the agency must look beyond healthcare delivery and ask how each part of the system supports combat power. He noted his fiscal year 2027 campaign order will finalize “the plan to deliver my four strategic priorities” — the agency’s “North Star” in optimizing operational medical readiness.

“To achieve our North Star, DHA should be synchronized and data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support,” Via said.

Agency’s focus on keeping warfighters healthy and lethal

Via stressed DHA needs to find ways to return the warfighter to the fight more quickly.

He described studies of musculoskeletal injuries finding gaps between healing and nondeployability, saying the insights offer a “chance to return more people to the fight faster.”

“We have to deliver the readiness of the warfighter,” Via declared.

He tied this goal to better access to care, faster referrals, and clearer measurable outcomes on meeting the mission, mobilizing leaders to use data to find root causes of illness or injury instead of only treating symptoms.

Via referenced the vital work of Dr. Jesus Caban, DHA’s chief data and analytics officer, and his team to make data more accessible, using artificial intelligence to translate a wealth of information into useful knowledge quickly. He noted this data and access to the Joint Medical Planning Tool, a computer-based simulation tool that models patient flow from point of injury through more definitive care, which can help predict casualties, support treatment and evacuation decisions, and guide supply and resupply in future battles — enhancing medical warrior currency across the enterprise.

Accountability and ‘smart risks for the warfighter’

In his intent to give network and military hospital and clinic leaders more authority to make and execute decisions, Via underlined, “Everyone should feel empowered to solve the problems at their lowest level. Period.”

“Find the root cause, identify solutions, execute and learn,” he said, while urging leaders to challenge assumptions: “Be willing to speak truth to power.”

Leaders should push risk up the chain, not down it, he added: “It is taking risk at the right levels … if we’re going to take the risk, I’m happy to own the risk.”

Preparing combatant commands for tomorrow’s fight

He highlighted plans to strengthen support for combatant commands and casualty receiving facilities. DHA is working to set requirements for medical supplies in the fight, using planning tools to estimate casualty needs, and expanding spaces inside military hospitals and clinics currently used for other purposes.

“We’re going to get those opened up. We’re going to get them functional. We’re going to have them ready,” he said.

Aligning with his warfighter-first focus, Via briefly mentioned working with the Joint Trauma System to optimize the military’s trauma learning system, ensuring the joint force can adapt faster to modern battlefield threats. JTS plays a critical role in delivering joint warfighting capabilities through unified trauma clinical care standards and data-driven medical logistics.

“We are also going to stand up a Joint Warfighter Health System — we're going to learn from the JTS. We’re going to use those same models to drive mental health, TBI (traumatic brain injury), and infectious disease,” he said. “We’re going to use the same continuous, data-driven process improvement to keep and save warfighters and keep them in the fight.

He closed by emphasizing the role of military medical leaders in battlefield success and ensuring all beneficiaries receive the high-quality healthcare they deserve.

“You all will save more lives on the future battlefield … you will keep more fighters in the fight, and that is how we will win the war.”

title: Congress must reject Pentagon budget split | Opinion - The Oklahoman
description:
Tucked inside the latest National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is a proposal to split the Defense Health Program budget into two distinct accounts: one for active-duty combat readiness, and another for civilian network care.
While the Pentagon frames this budget split as a quest for bookkeeping transparency, military retirees must hear the true subtext: The "One TRICARE" lifelong promise is being systematically dismantled.
The Pentagon is weaponizing the budget process to create tiers of an "earned benefit" based entirely on a birth certificate.
If this budget split passes, it will codify a permanent, three-tier hierarchy of care: Tier One: Active-duty personnel, whose care is legally protected for "readiness."
Congress must reject this budget split and instead codify a unified budget that reflects a unified promise.
text:
Mark Twain famously noted that history doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. For America’s military community, a dangerous refrain is playing out right now in Congress, echoing a breach of trust from decades ago.

Tucked inside the latest National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is a proposal to split the Defense Health Program budget into two distinct accounts: one for active-duty combat readiness, and another for civilian network care.

While the Pentagon frames this budget split as a quest for bookkeeping transparency, military retirees must hear the true subtext: The "One TRICARE" lifelong promise is being systematically dismantled.

In federal budgeting, financial silos are never just about math. Silos are about rationing.

We have seen this script before. Congress established CHAMPUS — TRICARE’s predecessor program — in 1966 to ensure military families and retirees were cared for. Decades later, when the government began forcing Medicare-eligible retirees out of that very system, it sparked a decade of "broken promise" lawsuits from veterans who were told their medical care was covered for life.

Today, the danger is already active. The Department of Defense currently exploits regulatory loopholes to abruptly revoke existing prior approvals and exclude TRICARE For Life (TFL) beneficiaries over age 65 from high-cost prescription coverage, even when clinically necessary.

A retiree over 65 is routinely denied the exact same medication fully covered for an active-duty member or a younger retiree with the exact same diagnosis.

Consider "Donna" in Utah, who used the TRICARE system to lose 100 pounds and eliminate her blood pressure medication. The day she turned 65, the system turned its back, cutting off the very treatment that made her a success story.

In Charleston, South Carolina, Dawn's husband served 31 years in uniform. Yet, they are watching their health care benefits vanish as his vital medications are stripped away simply because of his 65th birthday. The Pentagon is weaponizing the budget process to create tiers of an "earned benefit" based entirely on a birth certificate.

If this budget split passes, it will codify a permanent, three-tier hierarchy of care:

Tier One: Active-duty personnel, whose care is legally protected for "readiness."

Tier Two: Under-65 retirees, who face narrowing doctor networks and rising out-of-pocket costs.

Tier Three: Senior veterans over 65, relegated to whatever fiscal crumbs remain in a capped, secondary account.

When you split the money, you split the mission. It is a tactical retreat from a lifelong commitment to those who defended this nation.

There is a clear alternative. The One TRICARE Initiative has shared a legislative framework with Oklahoma delegates, Sen. James Lankford and U.S. Rep. Stephanie Bice, titled the "One TRICARE" Parity Principle. This amendment would ensure that if a treatment is clinically authorized under any TRICARE plan, it cannot be banned or rationed under another based on age.

We cannot allow quality of life to become a benefit with an expiration date. Congress must reject this budget split and instead codify a unified budget that reflects a unified promise. Anything less is a betrayal that rhymes far too closely with the broken promises of our past.

Fred Shakeshaft is the founder of OneTRICARE.org and a TRICARE For Life beneficiary. He is a retired Army staff sergeant with 42 years of combined U.S. Army and Civil Service experience. Throughout his career, he served as an AFN-TV studio director and produced multimedia products for USAREC, TRADOC, FORSCOM and the U.S. Army Airborne & Special Operations Museum.

Many pregnancies require additional monitoring and specialized care due to maternal or fetal health conditions. These conditions can include preexisting diabetes, gestational diabetes, high blood pressure or preeclampsia, advanced maternal age, autoimmune conditions, placental abnormalities, fetal anomalies, or fetal growth restriction. Our experienced providers work closely with you in conjunction with Maternal Fetal Medicine (MFM or High Risk OB) physicians to help ensure the healthiest pregnancy and delivery for you and your baby. You have many choices for MFM care in the Triangle region, and we regularly work closely with the care teams at Calla MFM in Raleigh, the University of Chapel Hill, and Duke practices.

Visit here to know more.

If you're having difficulty becoming pregnant, you're not alone. 10 women out of every 100 women in the United States struggle with infertility. It’s often frustrating and confusing, but you don’t have to face it alone. Our compassionate team offers initial infertility evaluations to help identify potential causes and develop a personalized plan for moving forward. We are committed to providing guidance, support, and appropriate treatment options or referrals to fertility specialists when needed.

At Cary OB/GYN, we will see you for your first visit around 7-8 weeks gestation to confirm the pregnancy and establish a due date with an ultrasound. The War Department recognized unique and innovative suicide prevention programs during a ceremony in the Pentagon's Hall of Heroes, Sept. 2.

The 11 department and two Coast Guard programs were recognized for building partnerships, equipping leaders and peers, connecting people with resources, and creating environments in which service members and families could more readily seek support.

"It is not just what they did during the last Suicide Prevention Month," said Alicia Matteson, Defense Suicide Prevention Office acting director. "They represent sustained efforts, informed by data, informed by the needs of their particular communities that they are serving."

Keith Bass, assistant secretary of war for health affairs, praised each of the honorees before handing out the awards.

"Today, we honor outstanding individuals for their efforts. I was just absolutely in awe of the creativity and the passion," Bass said. "Thank you on behalf of the Military Health System."

Joining Bass and Matteson during the annual event were Tim Hoyt, Defense Health Agency chief mental health officer, and Coast Guard Rear Adm. Shane Steiner, Coast Guard deputy assistant commandant for workforce and family services.

September may be Suicide Prevention Month, Hoyt noted, "but the individuals and commands we recognize today did not limit their work to a single month, event or campaign. They invested in suicide prevention throughout the year."

Hoyt added that celebrating these efforts today conveys to the force that the department values a multilayered approach to suicide prevention, which includes:

Leaders who know and care for their people.

Commands who act before concerns become a crisis.

Programs that make support easier to access.

Teams that strengthen connection and belonging.

The recognized programs represent a vital part in fostering that sense of support and connection in military communities, the speakers underscored.

Bass said when someone seeks care in a military hospital or clinic, "we will wrap our arms around that individual. We're going to take care of them and we're going to take care of our families. We have to continue to push this awareness. Nobody's alone. We do this as a team to take care of our folks."

During the ceremony, leaders emphasized that hope resounded throughout each team's efforts to prevent suicide.

"Hope is a belief that things will get better. But it's more than that," Matteson said. "It is also having the agency to make it so. And sometimes we forget that piece. The agency to make it so needs to exist for individuals to have hope that things will get better."

text:
WASHINGTON, DC — A proposed rule from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) is seeking to overhaul the uniform guidance for federal grantees. The rule would deemphasize the peer-review process, requiring grants to fall in line with administration priorities and be signed off on by political appointees. The initiative comes as morale among federal researchers, especially at VA, is reportedly at an all-time low due after 2 years of hiring freezes and staff cuts.

Should it go into effect, the new language would reshape grant regulations to reflect President Donald Trump’s executive orders targeting diversity initiatives and other “woke” causes.

“Federal grants funded unlawful DEI practices, various anti-American ideologies in American education, non-replicable and highly misleading studies, labs engaged in gain-of-function research, and AI-powered social media censorship tools,” OMB wrote in its executive summary of the proposed rule. “Grantmaking practices resulting in wasteful spending that became prevalent during the previous administration can only be stopped through adherence to strong internal controls at federal agencies.”

Deeper in the proposed rule, OMB states, “Discretionary awards must, where applicable, demonstrably advance the President’s policy priorities.”

The proposal, published in late May, received nearly a half-million comments, most of them being overwhelmingly negative.

“I don’t think, in my time that I’ve been privileged to serve in the Senate, that I have seen a rule, a proposed rule, generate that many negative comments,” declared Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME).

Her comments were made during a floor debate on the stopgap measure seeking to fund the government through the end of the year. The Senate version of the bill includes a provision temporarily blocking the OMB rule. Collins and others have called for some sections to be removed from the bill, while Democrats have called for it to be rescinded entirely.

The stopgap funding bill passed the Senate easily but still awaits a vote in the House, which will not reconvene until after Labor Day.

Meanwhile, lawmakers are still trying to measure the impact of last year’s staffing cuts and hiring freeze on researchers at VA.

“On the very first day of the Trump administration, all VA research staff became subject to a hiring freeze and probationary firings. As a result, research at the Pittsburgh VA to predict stroke risk was put on hold, enrollment into clinical trials for advanced cancer was delayed, and a clinical trial in Florida on preventing dementia and heart disease was cancelled,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA) said during a Senate VA Committee hearing examining the state of VA research. “The department also enforced vacancy cuts and staffing caps on its facilities. Though these cuts technically exclude research staff, a study at a VA site in the Pacific Northwest was delayed because staffing caps prevented them from hiring nurses who were needed to administer that study.”

According to Murray, VA researchers are reporting that startup times for studies can stretch to over a year and that hiring a new staff member often takes up to 6 months.

“A planned study on RSV missed its enrollment window and could not even enroll participants,” Murray declared. “Another clinical trial closed after it took six months to hire a researcher. The study’s principal investigator and its lead clinician both resigned from the VA after this debacle.”

The proposed OMB rule amounts to “one final blow to research,” she said. “That doesn’t make sense—letting political appointees overrule the scientist on what research is worth pursuing and funding.”

Glenn Graham, MD, former executive director of VA’s neurology clinical service, left VA in September 2025. He told the committee that before he left “staff were more upset and distracted and anxious than I have ever seen in my career.”

“Our researchers were concerned with hiring delays, with attrition of staff, particularly support staff which could be laboratory staff or clinical support or research office staff, as well with increased demands on physicians to devote themselves just to the clinical demands of VA and not get time for research,” Graham said.

There was also a pervasive fear of job loss, with staff fearing that, if they didn’t leave voluntarily, they would be pushed out during another reduction in force wave.

“When there were opportunities to take early retirement, there were good folks we lost in the organization. They were afraid if they didn’t take that option, they would be RIFed and they would have nothing,” Graham said.

This kind of pervasive fear is especially harmful in a healthcare environment, where distractions can result in patient harm, Graham told lawmakers. “In a healthcare organization, it’s very important that you have psychological safety, that you be a high reliability organization. You need to feel safe to report errors, to report potential areas where inefficiencies occur and harm can occur. In a context where people are more afraid of losing their job or being reprimanded or scapegoated, that doesn’t foster a culture of safety.”

text:
Bethesda, MD -- In collaboration with the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA), faculty members from the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (USU) have released a new, first of its kind, scientific statement to protect the heart health of tactical athletes (TAs), the first of its kind. “Clinical Considerations for the Care of the Tactical Athlete With Cardiovascular Abnormalities,” provides a formal framework for providing medical care to tactical athletes with cardiovascular risk or disease.

Tactical athletes include, but are not limited to, firefighters, law enforcement officers, astronauts, emergency medical personnel, and military personnel of diverse occupations. They operate under extreme physical demands yet have long faced a critical gap in health oversight. While many of the governing bodies for these TAs maintain their own medical standards, formal, unified guidance on occupational eligibility has long been lacking. This is especially concerning given that cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of duty-related death, often exacerbated by the unique environmental and physiological stressors inherent to tactical fields.

Building upon USU’s commitment to strengthen warfighter readiness, the scientific statement is a direct response to the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act, which required the Department of Defense to establish evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for cardiac screenings and treatment. A coalition of 50 experts in military and sports cardiology, including 13 current and former military physicians, first met in April 2024 at the ACC Heart House in Washington, DC. They then spent the next two years conducting a comprehensive literature review and synthesizing TA-focused data. Both the meeting and publication were funded by a grant from the Defense Health Agency to USU and the University’s Military Cardiovascular Outcomes Research (MiCOR) program through the Metis Foundation. The chairman of the meeting was Dr. Elizabeth Dineen (Mayo Clinic), and Drs. Mark Haigney (USU) and Ben Levine (U. Texas/Southwestern) were co-chairs.

“We hope this document will significantly aid clinicians caring for tactical athletes with conditions that currently are considered disqualifying for military service,” said Dr. Mark Haigney, director of MiCOR and the Department of Medicine’s Cardiology Division at USU. “In many cases, however, the underlying problem can be corrected or mitigated, allowing the TA to safely continue service without endangering the missions they are executing.”

The ACC/AHA’s new publication is organized into 11 specialized sections designed to assist providers navigate the complexities of caring for TAs living with cardiovascular disease or high-risk factors. Contributing authors and writers ensured individual TA health needs were balanced with organizational safety and medico-legal requirements. Key areas of focus include:

Mission-critical assessments: standardizing how "fitness for duty" is determined for high-stakes roles.

Advanced clinical management: developing guidance for screening for heart disease and for managing aortic aneurysm, myocarditis, congenital heart disease, coronary disease, and arrhythmias within a tactical context.

Emerging risks: evaluating environmental exposures and impact of performance-enhancing supplements.

Older tactical athletes: considering additional clinical protocols based on needs of a maturing workforce.

As an official statement of both the AHA and ACC, the publication in its entirety can be viewed at https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.07.003

* * *

About the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences: The Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, founded by an act of Congress in 1972, is the nation’s federal health sciences university and the academic heart of the Military Health System. USU students are primarily active-duty uniformed officers in the Army, Navy, Air Force and Public Health Service who receive specialized education in tropical and infectious diseases, TBI and PTSD, disaster response and humanitarian assistance, global health, and acute trauma care. USU also has graduate programs in oral biology, biomedical sciences and public health committed to excellence in research. The University's research program covers a wide range of areas important to both the military and public health. For more information about USU and its programs, visit www.usuhs.edu.

text:
The Defense Health Agency will launch a three-year pilot on Sept. 14, 206, to support eligible service members who want to freeze sperm or eggs through the Cryopreservation Demonstration Program — 30 days after being listed in the Federal Register.

Mandated by the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025, the demonstration program will reimburse certain costs tied to sperm or egg freezing, giving eligible service members more choice in family planning.

The program, overseen by the DHA medical affairs directorate, “offers support for members who face unique military demands,” said Air Force Maj. (Dr.) Kathleen Pombier, chief of DHA’s women’s health clinical management team. “Military service has an impact on how people build their families, with deployments and long separations affecting when troops decide to have children.”

Cryopreservation safely freezes eggs or sperm with liquid nitrogen to stop the aging process. The frozen eggs and sperm can be thawed, even years later, so service members can use them when the time better fits their family planning objectives, said Pombier.

Designed to give active duty service members “flexibility in choosing when to build their family,” cryopreservation can provide them with more “options in their reproductive future, or if there are issues with getting pregnant,” she said. By providing these family planning possibilities, the program ensures the delivery of high-quality care to all beneficiaries, Pombier added.

In DHA’s effort to deliver joint warfighting capabilities, the pilot covers all active duty forces — U.S. Army, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Air Force, and U.S Space Force. To be eligible, a service member must meet one of three conditions:

Have orders for duty that qualify for hazardous duty pay

Be likely to receive orders for duty that qualify for hazardous duty pay within 120 days

Who will, under orders, be geographically separated from a spouse, domestic partner, or dating partner for more than 180 days, including sea duty

The program is voluntary and not a TRICARE benefit, Pombier noted. Participants can be reimbursed up to $500 per year for sperm preservation and capped at $10,000 per year for egg preservation. The demonstration program will also reimburse for related medications, medical tests, lab work, and imaging. Storage and shipping causes may also be reimbursed. Embryo creation, in vitro fertilization, or other elective procedures are not covered.

“We encourage participants to use a participating military hospital or clinic,” said Pombier, but a civilian fertility clinic may also be used, and doesn’t have to be TRICARE-authorized.

Participants must follow timing guidelines: All testing, retrieval, and freezing generally must occur before orders begin. Beneficiaries who face a qualifying long separation may receive services before the separation or while it continues, if care is available.

Pombier said those interested should begin with the DHA’s program website to get started. All service members must get confirmation of eligibility from their commander before seeking reimbursement. An advance medical directive is also required of all participants stating how they want their stored sperm or eggs handled if they die.

Throughout the demonstration program phase, DHA will track use, costs, claims processing, patient experience, and impact on readiness and retention — all part of a feasibility assessment, Pombier said.

The program is set to end after the initial three-year mandate, unless it’s extended. Pombier said eligible participants should expect to pay storage and shipping costs after the pilot ends if the program doesn’t continue.

In providing “eligible service members options to choose when to begin a family,” the program delivers warfighter medical readiness by allowing them to “focus more on being mission-ready rather than worrying about family planning,” said Pombier.

text:
‘North Star’ of Defense Health Agency is data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support, declares director

Defense Health Agency

Story by Robert Hammer

Date: 09.08.2026

Posted: 09.08.2026 14:01

News ID: 574098

To a cohort of emerging military healthcare leaders at the 2026 Tri-Service Chapters Annual Scientific Meeting, Defense Health Agency Director Navy Vice Adm. Darin K. Via positioned the agency as a source of “problem solvers and solution providers” to optimize combat support in generating and sustaining global warfighter readiness.

In his remarks at the meeting in Bethesda, Maryland, Aug. 26, Via called upon future leaders across the military healthcare enterprise to own risk, solve problems at the right level, and focus on ensuring service members are medically ready for the future fight.

“Military medicine faces a more complex future than it did during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan,” Via said. “The enemy has changed the tactics on us, and we have to adapt,” in delivering care to warfighters.

The joint medical education conference is hosted by the American College of Physicians for military internal medicine professionals, including physicians, residents, fellows, and other healthcare professionals.

Via said since the first day he became director of the agency, his goal was to make “the entire DHA a combat support agency.”

His viewpoint shapes how DHA leaders will measure success, Via said, emphasizing the agency must look beyond healthcare delivery and ask how each part of the system supports combat power. He noted his fiscal year 2027 campaign order will finalize “the plan to deliver my four strategic priorities” — the agency’s “North Star” in optimizing operational medical readiness.

“To achieve our North Star, DHA should be synchronized and data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support,” Via said.

Agency’s focus on keeping warfighters healthy and lethal

Via stressed DHA needs to find ways to return the warfighter to the fight more quickly.

He described studies of musculoskeletal injuries finding gaps between healing and nondeployability, saying the insights offer a “chance to return more people to the fight faster.”

“We have to deliver the readiness of the warfighter,” Via declared.

He tied this goal to better access to care, faster referrals, and clearer measurable outcomes on meeting the mission, mobilizing leaders to use data to find root causes of illness or injury instead of only treating symptoms.

Via referenced the vital work of Dr. Jesus Caban, DHA’s chief data and analytics officer, and his team to make data more accessible, using artificial intelligence to translate a wealth of information into useful knowledge quickly. He noted this data and access to the Joint Medical Planning Tool, a computer-based simulation tool that models patient flow from point of injury through more definitive care, which can help predict casualties, support treatment and evacuation decisions, and guide supply and resupply in future battles — enhancing medical warrior currency across the enterprise.

Accountability and ‘smart risks for the warfighter’

In his intent to give network and military hospital and clinic leaders more authority to make and execute decisions, Via underlined, “Everyone should feel empowered to solve the problems at their lowest level. Period.”

“Find the root cause, identify solutions, execute and learn,” he said, while urging leaders to challenge assumptions: “Be willing to speak truth to power.”

Leaders should push risk up the chain, not down it, he added: “It is taking risk at the right levels … if we’re going to take the risk, I’m happy to own the risk.”

Preparing combatant commands for tomorrow’s fight

He highlighted plans to strengthen support for combatant commands and casualty receiving facilities. DHA is working to set requirements for medical supplies in the fight, using planning tools to estimate casualty needs, and expanding spaces inside military hospitals and clinics currently used for other purposes.

“We’re going to get those opened up. We’re going to get them functional. We’re going to have them ready,” he said.

Aligning with his warfighter-first focus, Via briefly mentioned working with the Joint Trauma System to optimize the military’s trauma learning system, ensuring the joint force can adapt faster to modern battlefield threats. JTS plays a critical role in delivering joint warfighting capabilities through unified trauma clinical care standards and data-driven medical logistics.

“We are also going to stand up a Joint Warfighter Health System — we're going to learn from the JTS. We’re going to use those same models to drive mental health, TBI (traumatic brain injury), and infectious disease,” he said. “We’re going to use the same continuous, data-driven process improvement to keep and save warfighters and keep them in the fight.

He closed by emphasizing the role of military medical leaders in battlefield success and ensuring all beneficiaries receive the high-quality healthcare they deserve.

“You all will save more lives on the future battlefield … you will keep more fighters in the fight, and that is how we will win the war.”

Agency’s focus on keeping warfighters healthy and lethal

Via stressed DHA needs to find ways to return the warfighter to the fight more quickly.

He described studies of musculoskeletal injuries finding gaps between healing and nondeployability, saying the insights offer a “chance to return more people to the fight faster.”

“We have to deliver the readiness of the warfighter,” Via declared.

He tied this goal to better access to care, faster referrals, and clearer measurable outcomes on meeting the mission, mobilizing leaders to use data to find root causes of illness or injury instead of only treating symptoms.

Via referenced the vital work of Dr. Jesus Caban, DHA’s chief data and analytics officer, and his team to make data more accessible, using artificial intelligence to translate a wealth of information into useful knowledge quickly. He noted this data and access to the Joint Medical Planning Tool, a computer-based simulation tool that models patient flow from point of injury through more definitive care, which can help predict casualties, support treatment and evacuation decisions, and guide supply and resupply in future battles — enhancing medical warrior currency across the enterprise.

Accountability and ‘smart risks for the warfighter’

In his intent to give network and military hospital and clinic leaders more authority to make and execute decisions, Via underlined, “Everyone should feel empowered to solve the problems at their lowest level. Period.”

“Find the root cause, identify solutions, execute and learn,” he said, while urging leaders to challenge assumptions: “Be willing to speak truth to power.”

Leaders should push risk up the chain, not down it, he added: “It is taking risk at the right levels … if we’re going to take the risk, I’m happy to own the risk.”

Preparing combatant commands for tomorrow’s fight

He highlighted plans to strengthen support for combatant commands and casualty receiving facilities. DHA is working to set requirements for medical supplies in the fight, using planning tools to estimate casualty needs, and expanding spaces inside military hospitals and clinics currently used for other purposes.

“We’re going to get those opened up. We’re going to get them functional. We’re going to have them ready,” he said.

Aligning with his warfighter-first focus, Via briefly mentioned working with the Joint Trauma System to optimize the military’s trauma learning system, ensuring the joint force can adapt faster to modern battlefield threats. JTS plays a critical role in delivering joint warfighting capabilities through unified trauma clinical care standards and data-driven medical logistics.

“We are also going to stand up a Joint Warfighter Health System — we're going to learn from the JTS. We’re going to use those same models to drive mental health, TBI (traumatic brain injury), and infectious disease,” he said. “We’re going to use the same continuous, data-driven process improvement to keep and save warfighters and keep them in the fight.

He closed by emphasizing the role of military medical leaders in battlefield success and ensuring all beneficiaries receive the high-quality healthcare they deserve.

“You all will save more lives on the future battlefield … you will keep more fighters in the fight, and that is how we will win the war.”

Assets and planned payments

His assets include $500,000 in stocks, ETFs, index and mutual funds; $330,000 in 401(k) and Thrift Savings Plan accounts; $295,000 in certificates of deposit; $180,000 in savings; $117,000 in a deferred annuity; $97,000 in Series I savings bonds; and $10,000 in cash. The man plans to leave federal service at age 62, with approximately 33 years of creditable service in the Federal Employees Retirement System after making military service deposits. He expects to retain Federal Employees Health Benefits health insurance, FEGLI life insurance and TRICARE health coverage. By his estimate, at age 68, at the end of December 2035, he will be able to receive $2,431 per month from Social Security.

title: Pentagon Reportedly Using Medical Records to Identify Transgender Troops - Military.com
description:
The Pentagon is using military medical and personnel records to identify service members with current or past diagnoses of gender dysphoria as it moves to separate transgender troops under the Trump administration's ban, according to a Federal News Network investigation published Monday.
The Pentagon, Defense Health Agency and individual military services declined to answer Federal News Network's questions about the process, citing ongoing litigation.
How the Pentagon Is Identifying Service Members Defense officials have previously acknowledged that medical information would play a role in identifying troops subject to separation.
What Military Medical Privacy Rules Allow The reported use of medical records raises questions about how much of a service member's health information can be shared with commanders.
Attorneys representing the service members argue the policy unlawfully discriminates against transgender troops and excludes people who are otherwise capable of meeting military standards.
text:
The Pentagon is using military medical and personnel records to identify service members with current or past diagnoses of gender dysphoria as it moves to separate transgender troops under the Trump administration's ban, according to a Federal News Network investigation published Monday.

The effort has led commanders across the military to receive notices identifying troops in their units who may fall under the policy and directing them to begin the separation process, per the report. The outlet cited multiple service members, advocates and internal military documents.

An internal Air Force email obtained by Federal News Network said the Office of the Secretary of Defense had identified service members "who may have a current diagnosis or history of or exhibit symptoms consistent with gender dysphoria in their electronic healthcare record."

The Pentagon, Defense Health Agency and individual military services declined to answer Federal News Network's questions about the process, citing ongoing litigation.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to Military.com's request for comment on Monday.

The latest reporting offers a clearer picture of how the Pentagon is identifying service members who did not voluntarily come forward after the department began implementing its transgender service ban last year.

How the Pentagon Is Identifying Service Members

Defense officials have previously acknowledged that medical information would play a role in identifying troops subject to separation.

In May 2025, a senior defense official said the Individual Medical Readiness program would be the "primary means" of determining whether service members meet the new medical standards.

Under the policy, troops with a current diagnosis or history of gender dysphoria—or symptoms consistent with the condition—are generally disqualified from continued military service unless they receive a waiver.

The Pentagon estimated in May 2025 that roughly 4,200 service members had been diagnosed with gender dysphoria, though officials acknowledged the figure could have changed.

Defense officials said at the time that commanders who were already aware of a service member who met the criteria could direct an individualized review of that person's medical records. The department also said troops would be evaluated through routine health screenings as they cycled through annual medical readiness requirements.

But Federal News Network's reporting indicates identification is also occurring at higher levels of the Pentagon, reaching commanders through information contained in electronic medical records.

Sources who spoke with the outlet claim officials are using MHS Genesis, the Pentagon's electronic health record system, as well as other military databases.

MHS Genesis supports more than 9.5 million military health system beneficiaries, including service members, military retirees and family members, and is designed to provide a single electronic health record across military care.

It was reported that one separation referral sent to an airman's commander included information about the service member's previous treatment, including counseling and medication.

The airman told the outlet they were not currently experiencing gender dysphoria and had not disclosed their past treatment to colleagues.

What Military Medical Privacy Rules Allow

The reported use of medical records raises questions about how much of a service member's health information can be shared with commanders.

Military health information is generally protected by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, but the law includes an exception for certain disclosures involving members of the armed forces.

Under what the Defense Health Agency calls the "Military Command Exception," military health providers may disclose protected health information to command authorities for authorized activities, including determining fitness for duty, fitness to perform a particular assignment or other activities necessary to the military mission.

The exception does not give commanders unrestricted access to medical records.

The Defense Health Agency says health information disclosed under the command exception is no longer protected by HIPAA once provided to military command authorities, but remains protected under the Privacy Act of 1974.

Separate Defense Department rules generally restrict command notification when a service member receives mental health or substance abuse treatment unless certain circumstances apply, including a serious risk of harm to the service member, others or the military mission.

During a May 2025 Pentagon briefing, a senior defense official said commanders would be required to protect medical information received as part of the transgender separation policy.

The official also said the Pentagon remained "committed to protecting both their privacy and their medical data."

An internal Army order issued in August explicitly limits how commanders themselves can search for affected soldiers. The order bars commanders from broadly searching health and personnel records for soldiers with gender dysphoria or asking medical providers for batches of information about members of their units, according to the outlet.

However, commanders can act on information sent from higher headquarters indicating that a soldier's medical record contains a past diagnostic code associated with gender dysphoria.

The Army order also reportedly directs medical providers to notify commanders when annual physicals identify a current or past diagnosis.

Separations Continue as the Policy Faces Court Challenges

The Pentagon began implementing the current policy after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in January 2025 directing the military to change its standards for transgender service members.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth subsequently issued guidance barring people with a current diagnosis or history of gender dysphoria, or symptoms consistent with it, from military service except under limited circumstances.

The Pentagon later offered affected active-duty and reserve troops periods in which they could identify themselves and voluntarily separate before the military moved toward involuntary separations for those who remained.

The policy has faced multiple federal court challenges since shortly after Trump issued the executive order in January 2025.

In May 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the Pentagon to enforce the policy while litigation in Shilling v. United States continued, staying a preliminary injunction issued by a federal judge in Washington state. The Supreme Court did not rule at that stage on whether the policy itself was constitutional.

A separate challenge, Talbott v. United States, remains pending. In June 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction protecting the current service-member plaintiffs in that case while narrowing the scope of the lower court's order.

The Trump administration filed a petition with the Supreme Court on Aug. 27 asking the justices to review the D.C. Circuit's ruling.

The government argues that decisions about medical qualifications for military service warrant significant judicial deference and that the policy does not violate the Fifth Amendment's equal-protection guarantee.

Attorneys representing the service members argue the policy unlawfully discriminates against transgender troops and excludes people who are otherwise capable of meeting military standards.

The new identification effort is affecting active-duty and reserve personnel, as well as service academy and ROTC cadets, according to Federal News Network.

SPARTA Pride, an advocacy organization for transgender service members, and an attorney representing affected troops told the outlet that several hundred people may have been identified through the process during the past two months.

The Defense Department has not publicly confirmed that figure.

text:
The US Department of Defense has temporarily rescinded clinical guidance on implementing mandatory testosterone deficiency screenings for active-duty and reserve service members aged 30 and older.

The Defense Health Agency published the directive in early September before removing the documents from its website the following day.

Officials confirmed the interim guidance remains active while final clinical rules undergo updates.

“What was posted earlier this week was something that was a draft,” ABC News quoted US Defense Secretary Senior Advisor Tim Parlatore as saying. “It was not approved for release. Somebody had put it out there inadvertently.”

The move comes after Pentagon Chief Pete Hegseth ordered the program last July, framing hormone optimization as essential to maintaining “biological foundation required to sustain the fight.”

The pulled document established yearly evaluations consisting of questionnaires and blood tests for male service members over 30, while younger troops would undergo testing only upon request or clinical indication.

The paper also outlined annual hormone-related health evaluations for female service members.

Reaction From Medical Community

Medical specialists have criticized universal hormone screening across healthy populations, citing a lack of evidence that broad testing enhances military readiness, according to Reuters.

Experts also warned that unnecessary testosterone replacement therapy carries risks, including cardiovascular issues, sleep apnea, and infertility.

Neither the Endocrine Society nor the American Urological Association recommends routine testing for asymptomatic individuals.

The policy was launched ahead of a scheduled mid-September Food and Drug Administration expert panel convened to discuss the medical uses and safety of testosterone.

Washington did not provide a timeline for releasing the finalized guidance.

text:
Retired U.S. Army officer and leadership strategist delivers two-day intensive, "Eliminating Operational Chaos Through Strategic Leadership," built on her Battle-Tested Leadership Methodology™

WASHINGTON, D.C. - 07 September, 2026 - Dr. Traci Eisenberg-Rayburn, founder of E&R Business Consulting and a retired U.S. Army officer who once led soldiers in uniform, spent August 12 and 13 in front of a very different formation: supervisors at the Defense Health Agency. The two-day engagement brought her Battle-Tested Leadership Methodology™ to a federal audience carrying the same operational pressures she once managed in uniform: high stakes, constant competition for attention, and very little room for direction to get lost on the way down.

As an immersive keynote speaker, business strategist, and leadership coach, Dr. Traci delivered Eliminating Operational Chaos Through Strategic Leadership, a two-day leadership intensive built on her signature Battle-Tested Leadership Methodology™. Rather than a general session on management theory, the program was built around a specific, recurring problem supervisors raise across industries: teams that work hard but still produce inconsistent results, because the structure underneath the effort was never built to hold it.

The two days ran as working sessions rather than lectures. Supervisors brought a real project they were currently managing, built it out with their hands, took it apart, and rebuilt it toward what the work becomes next rather than what it looks like today.

Around that exercise, the program worked four mechanics of consistent execution: how direction holds its shape as it moves through an organization, and where the message erodes between what a leader intends and what reaches the front line; how trust is built on predictability rather than personality, so a team's confidence does not rise and fall with someone's mood that day; how an expectation becomes specific enough that accountability is not a matter of interpretation; and how a leader names the style she defaults to under pressure, rather than reaching for whatever habit shows up when the workload gets heavy.

The two days centered on leadership of the work and leadership of the people doing it. Instead of sitting through slides, supervisors practiced setting expectations clearly enough that accountability is not left to interpretation, communicating direction so it survives the trip from the leadership layer to the front line, and listening in a way that changes what they hear from their teams. Each left with written commitments tied to their own people, and a method they can run again without a facilitator in the room. Dr. Traci returns in September to carry the same work into the supervisors' teams.

“You already work hard. That has never been the question. The question is whether the work is structured to succeed.”

~ Dr. Traci Eisenberg-Rayburn, Founder, E&R Business Consulting

That line sits at the center of how Dr. Traci approaches leadership work: the issue in most struggling teams is rarely effort. It's structure. Supervisors are frequently working as hard as they can inside a system that was never designed to convert that effort into predictable results — and that gap, left unaddressed, tends to get quietly absorbed by the same handful of people until it eventually shows up as turnover, missed deadlines, or leadership burnout.

Dr. Traci’s approach draws directly on her military background, where she spent a career moving intent into action across layers of command, under conditions where ambiguity carries real cost. She has since built that experience into a methodology aimed at organizations outside the military that are dealing with a civilian version of the same challenge: good people, real effort, and a structure that isn't yet built to match it.

Dr. Traci Eisenberg-Rayburn works with organizations that are already performing and want their leadership to scale with them, so growth stays consistent instead of dependent on who happens to be in the room on a given day. That distinction, between leadership that depends on a specific individual and leadership that holds up regardless of who is leading, sits at the center of the Battle-Tested Leadership Methodology™. It is the same throughline connecting this engagement with the Defense Health Agency to the broader body of work E&R Business Consulting has built with organizations navigating growth, transition, or operational strain.

The sweep is believed to have outed several hundred active-duty and reserve troops, including service academy and Reserve Officer Training Corps cadets, over the past two months, according to the trans advocacy nonprofit SPARTA Pride and Priya Rashid, an attorney with the National Institute of Military Justice.

The Pentagon is moving to separate troops as multiple lawsuits challenging the ban move through the federal court system. In August, the administration petitioned the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether the policy is unconstitutional before a key case goes to trial in January.

The situation has spurred a military-wide scramble to cover the work of troops placed on leave, connect them with legal help and, in some cases, find money and lodging for those facing homelessness.

“The military was my life; it was my everything. I gave my entire self to my job and to my country, and I was serious about my career,” one sailor said. “They’re about to completely upend my life and my career, and I’m not prepared for that.”

Finding trans troops

The Trump administration argues that any history of gender dysphoria, the medical condition where a person’s gender identity doesn’t match their biological sex, is incompatible with “high standards for troop readiness, lethality, cohesion, honesty, humility, uniformity and integrity.”

After President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, the Pentagon issued directives that formed the basis of the ban. It initially allowed troops to leave during a grace period that ended in July 2025, then began removing them itself.

Now SPARTA officials say dozens of people have reached out to report “unprecedented use of military medical systems to identify individuals.”

Five sources, including two transgender service members facing separation after their gender dysphoria-related diagnoses were flagged to their commands, described what they called a “witch hunt” for honorably serving troops. Three were granted anonymity because they fear retaliation.

Documents obtained by Federal News Network indicate that, in some cases, the information is coming from the Pentagon’s highest echelon.

The Office of the Secretary of Defense has identified service members “who may have a current diagnosis or history of or exhibit symptoms consistent with gender dysphoria in their electronic healthcare record,” according to an internal Air Force email sent July 31 and viewed by Federal News Network.

Spokespeople for the Defense Department, the Defense Health Agency and each of the military services declined to answer emailed questions, citing ongoing litigation.

Sources believe the military is digging through MHS Genesis, DoD’s electronic health records system, and other databases to find remaining transgender troops. The system contains medical histories, prescriptions, mental health notes, TRICARE-covered civilian care documentation and even records from before members joined the military. Personnel databases can also reveal changes in a person’s listed gender over time.

Some, but not all, transgender people experience gender dysphoria; it can be resolved through treatment. Kara Corcoran, SPARTA’s executive director, who is an active-duty Army infantry officer facing separation, said people are being punished for successfully addressing a past medical issue.

“A new line has just shifted and said that these people are inadequate for being able to serve,” she said.

Those details are being shared with unit leaders across the force in conversations and memos from local medical and legal offices, alarming some who argue it violates troops’ privacy and doctor-patient confidentiality.

One separation referral sent to an airman’s commander quoted directly from the service member’s health history, including when they sought treatment for gender dysphoria, their number of counseling sessions and prescribed medication.

The airman said they were never evaluated in order to receive the separation referral, do not currently experience dysphoria and had not shared details of their past treatment with their colleagues.

A widening sweep

SPARTA estimates thousands of trans troops have been kicked out or are in the process of separating, including those placed on leave until their discharge.

Still, it’s difficult to pinpoint the number of service members who identify as transgender. DoD estimated around 4,200 troops with gender dysphoria were in uniform when the ban began. That’s about four times higher than in 2019, when the department told a congressional defense committee that about 1,000 currently serving troops were diagnosed with at least one of seven medical codes related to the condition — a figure pulled from Military Health System data. Other outside estimates have ranged from about 6,000 to as many as 25,000 people.

Out trans members who publicly transitioned were among the first to go when the policy changes began. But that’s no longer the case in the ban’s second year, sources said.

Rashid, who represents many of the trans troops in their separation cases, said her calls have exploded over the past two months, with about 25 people reaching out each week for advice on involuntary separation procedures.

She said she’s heard from many troops younger than 21 who transitioned before joining the military and served in accordance with regulations for their preferred gender from the start.

The latest phase is also flagging older people who transitioned years ago, when they could do so without penalties, and whose current colleagues may not know. The Pentagon is identifying people whose medical notes reference a current or previous transition but who haven’t changed their names or gender markers, as well as those who continue to meet the appearance and fitness requirements of their biological sex.

They are also identifying troops diagnosed with gender dysphoria who didn’t transition, those who sought treatment outside the military but used TRICARE, and those who detransitioned to save their jobs.

“They didn’t do anything wrong,” Rashid said. “They followed the rules and policies and procedures of the year that they were in. We were the ones who changed the rules on them.”

The search is also catching people who aren’t transgender, she said, including members who underwent procedures such as mastectomies or hysterectomies or sought a gender dysphoria diagnosis to obtain treatment for other conditions.

The cost of separation

The airman and sailor who spoke to Federal News Network after their commands were told to remove them are grappling with the policy’s repercussions for their lives and for the units and country they serve.

Neither opted for a voluntary separation, a term many dislike because it implies they want to cut their military career short.

“I gave my word and swore an oath to my country … to serve my country honorably and to be an asset to the Navy’s warfighting capabilities,” the sailor said. “To voluntarily step away from that felt like a betrayal and a slap in the face to the Navy.”

While the Air Force appears to be processing cases through the medical establishment, the sailor said their local legal staff told them they meet the requirements for administrative separation. They believe their psychiatric records were searched for notes from clinical visits where they confidentially discussed a desire to transition.

Leaving the military would rob their unit of critical combat systems expertise others don’t have, they said. Shipmates who are underway have continued to call for technical support, forcing the sailor to “basically act as customer service over the phone to a ship in the middle of the ocean.”

“For both transgender service members and people who have served with them, we’re all absolutely f***ing livid,” the sailor said. “We have an absolute manning crisis… The more sailors you take off of these ships, transgender or not, you are directly contributing to them not being able to meet mission requirements.”

The airman knows they could earn more in the private sector but worries their departure could hurt the unit’s readiness and cohesion. They’re relieved they might soon be able to openly live as transgender, while grieving the loss of a life and career they love.

“‘My God, it’s finally over, and it wasn’t because I quit,’” the airman recalled thinking when they were told of their pending discharge. “I never gave up.”

What the military can see

MHS Genesis hosts the patient data of more than 9.5 million troops, spouses and children. Authorized users can search military health databases by diagnosis code to identify people with a certain condition and create registries of patients with particular ailments.

For instance, Military Health System software has been used to track outbreaks of communicable diseases, and identify people at high risk for bone marrow abnormalities.

MHS records have also been used to research service members with gender dysphoria-related diagnoses before. The 2019 report to the House Armed Services Committee lists the specific codes used to identify troops in the MHS Data Repository, including five that fall under gender dysphoria, one for cross-dressing fetishes and one for a history of sex reassignment.

Military medical providers have also relied on that data for studies on issues like inequities in hormone prescriptions for active-duty troops with a gender dysphoria-related diagnosis.

Health privacy laws are more complicated inside the U.S. military. To ensure enough troops are fit for duty at any given moment, HIPAA allows military treatment facilities to disclose protected health information to a service member’s command.

But the Military Health System says that information remains protected under the Privacy Act of 1974, which generally bars disclosure without written consent except in certain circumstances. Those exceptions include cases where an agency’s employees “have a need for the record in the performance of their duties,” according to statute.

The administration appears to be relying on a provision of the 2023 National Defense Authorization Act designed to reduce the stigma around mental health treatment, Rashid said. Congress directed the Defense Department to protect the confidentiality of mental health services except in exigent circumstances. That can allow disclosure when national security, safety or good order and discipline are at stake.

Rashid argues those exceptions don’t apply to transgender troops being removed from the military, including F-35 avionics technicians, pilots, air defenders and surgeons.

“These are zero-fail tasks that would require a high level of occupational finesse, a high level of technical proficiency,” she said. “Mentally unwell people would have a very difficult time.”

The separation process

The Pentagon’s initial guidance on identifying trans troops explicitly said it would do so using medical records. That’s evolved over time.

A March 2025 DoD memo noted that reviewing medical records would be the “primary means” of identifying troops with a history of gender dysphoria. Two months later, another memo clarified that the services should look to troops’ annual checkups and bloodwork to find instances of dysphoria.

“The secretaries of the military departments will direct unit commanders — working in coordination with supporting medical assets — to ensure service members comply with their [Individual Medical Readiness] program obligations and will immediately commence the identification of affected service members,” the May 2025 memo said.

“Commanders who are aware of service members in their units with gender dysphoria, a history of gender dysphoria, or symptoms consistent with gender dysphoria will direct individualized medical record reviews of such service members to confirm compliance with medical standards under the IMR program,” it added.

That process looks slightly different in each branch of the armed forces. An internal Army order, which was issued in August but was not made public, formalizes a monthslong blueprint for ousting soldiers.

The order, obtained by Federal News Network, explicitly bars commanders from broadly searching health and personnel records to find soldiers with gender dysphoria, or from asking providers for a batch of information about the people in their unit.

It also stops leaders from ordering a behavioral health consult to confirm whether a person has gender dysphoria unless they have personal knowledge of the diagnosis. That could stem from past conversations with the soldier, their request to follow different grooming standards, social media posts, or “reports from higher headquarters to commanders indicating an individual’s medical records reflect a past diagnostic code consistent with gender dysphoria.”

The Army noted that the form used at annual physicals now includes questions about gender dysphoria, and tells medical providers to immediately notify commanders of members with current or past gender dysphoria. And it tells commanders to update personnel records to reflect the biological sex of all soldiers, not only those pending separation.

Once a commander has verified that a soldier meets the criteria for separation, they must consult with their legal office and speak with the soldier to start the process.

Units have 30 days to process a soldier for separation after their gender dysphoria diagnosis or symptoms are verified, the memo says. If the soldier opts into a separation board, the hearing must take place no later than 60 days after the board receives the medical confirmation.

“Anyone who gets notified should be talking to Trial Defense Service that week — not after they’ve had time to sit with it,” Corcoran said.

The board’s decision heads to the Army secretary or another authority tapped to approve separations. The service has 90 days to kick out a soldier after authorizing their separation.

Commands across the Army must report their progress to service headquarters twice a month, including separation board dates.

In the Air Force and Space Force, medical readiness boards will determine whether airmen qualify for separation before sending cases to unit commanders, according to the internal email. Commanders then have three business days to send paperwork to a centralized legal team in Washington.

The Navy and Marine Corps have similar processes, with Navy Installations Command handling involuntary separations. Sailors have 10 days to request a separation board or waive that right.

The boards are directed to decide only whether someone was diagnosed with or has symptoms of gender dysphoria, regardless of their character or their job performance. Each service secretary makes the final call on whether to remove them.

At first, the airman debated whether they wanted to face a separation board, calling them “foregone conclusions.” But they want their service to make a difference.

“If my fight can help pave the way for others to freely serve in the future, then it’s absolutely worth it,” they said.

What happens next

Separation measures have continued as trans troops await a federal district court’s decision on who will be covered by a class-action lawsuit.

Lawyers representing more than two dozen service members warned last month that the Pentagon is expediting removals while a key lawsuit is tied up in appeals. In June, a federal judge allowed Talbott v. USA to become a class action but has not yet said who qualifies to join. The judge’s March 2025 order pausing separations has not taken effect amid administration pushback.

“The government is moving forward with involuntary separations of plaintiffs in this case,” plaintiff attorneys told the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit Aug. 17. “For example, the government postponed Lieutenant Junior Grade Clara Winchell’s board of inquiry following the issuance of this court’s opinion, but is now attempting to reschedule it to be held on or before Sept. 15, 2026.”

The Trump administration last month petitioned the Supreme Court to overrule the lower court and let it proceed with separations.

“The authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance,” the Justice Department wrote. “The court should thus take this opportunity to address the constitutionality of the Hegseth policy and reverse the decision.”

Corcoran said junior enlisted troops are among the most at risk. Those who have served less than six years are ineligible for separation pay, may have to repay part of their enlistment bonus, are last in line for veterans benefits and could become homeless.

SPARTA has provided more than $36,000 in financial support to 29 recipients so far this year, including four who used the money to leave states with anti-trans laws.

The airman and the sailor who spoke to Federal News Network both said they’d like to rejoin the military if separated. Current policy bars them from doing so.

“We’ll have our ups, we’ll have our downs, but at the end of the day, I’m still a United States Navy sailor, and I’m more than happy to wear my country’s flag on my shoulder,” the sailor said.

Abstract

This article evaluates the Defense Health Agency's (DHA) large animal Combat Casualty Care Research Program (CCCRP) at the David Grant Medical Center (DGMC) Clinical Investigation Program (CIP) as a dual-purpose model that advances military medical research and enhances surgical training for military residents. Over five years, residents performed thousands of emergency general surgery-equivalent procedures on large animals, gaining critical operative trauma and critical care experience that often exceeded Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) minimum requirements. The CCCRP provides a unique environment for maintaining and expanding expeditionary surgical skills amid declining clinical trauma exposure, while also supporting multidisciplinary training and research aligned with DHA and Department of Defense priorities. The study highlights the program's role in bridging research and hands-on training, emphasizing its value in preparing military surgeons for deployment without replacing human clinical experience.
